questions.question: A creator writes a new file whose directory contains exactly one top-level record: a user-metadata record with the smallest inline payload and the smallest permitted extent (inline_length = 1; extent_length = 5), and otherwise the smallest layout the format permits (dir_offset placed immediately after that record's extent, dir_length as small as the record framing allows, and the shortest legal pre-trailer pad). What is the minimum possible total file size in bytes?
questions.answer_form: a single integer (bytes)
questions.why_it_matters: Combines the 24-byte record header (§7.2), the fixed 1-byte user-metadata inline payload (§18.2), the extent_length >= 5 floor (§7.1), and the 64-byte trailer alignment/pad rule (§6.2) to show the file can still hit the bare 128-byte floor (§5.1/R-CNT-27) even while carrying a real record — a non-obvious result a table lookup alone would not reveal.

questions.question: A file's trailer declares version_major = 0. Does the invariant-'reach' analysis that decides which requirements apply to a file declaring a format major other than 1 apply to this file? Name the reader outcome class and the exact register row that governs this file instead.
questions.answer_form: a yes/no verdict plus an outcome-class name and a row label, e.g. "no; reject-file, F18"
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the stated exception that version_major = 0 'declares no major at all,' so the reach premise is unmet and the file is governed directly by R-CNT-07/F18 rather than by the R-CNT-24 reach machinery — a carve-out easily lost in a rewording.

questions.question: An appender is committing to a file whose current live trailer has flags bit 20 (an ignore-lane bit this specification's text assigns no meaning to) set to 1. In the new trailer this commit produces: (a) what must bit 20 be, and (b) is the appender permitted to additionally set flags bit 25 (also in the ignore lane, currently 0) to 1 in the new trailer?
questions.answer_form: two verdicts in order, e.g. "(a) 1; (b) not permitted"
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the carve-out that an updater must copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits unchanged and must never originate a new one — a rule split across §6.3's flag-gate text and §20.1's writer-tier framing.

questions.question: A file is created (its first generation) at the smallest size a conforming file can be, then undergoes exactly one further commit. What is the smallest possible committed_file_length its second generation's trailer can declare?
questions.answer_form: a single integer (bytes)
questions.why_it_matters: Combines the 128-byte absolute floor (§5.1/R-CNT-27) with the commit protocol's derived 'at least 128 more than the prior F' bound (§9.2's second Note) — neither section alone yields the number.

questions.question: A non-layer top-level record has extent_offset = 0 and extent_length = 40. Under the register's classification, which single row governs this file — F30 or F31 — and what is the reader outcome?
questions.answer_form: a row label plus an outcome-class name, e.g. "F30; reject-file"
questions.why_it_matters: F30 and F31 look superficially adjacent (both are extent-slot malformations), but F33's parenthetical explicitly assigns a zero-offset/nonzero-length slot to F30 rather than F31 — a disambiguation stated once, in passing, inside a different row's text.

questions.question: A layer stored at least one tile in generation N. Generation N+1's single commit both unstores every one of the layer's tiles (so the layer addresses tiles but stores none, i.e. becomes empty) and changes the layer's declared fill value for one channel. Is this a valid appender commit, or does it require declaring a new layer or performing a whole-file rewrite?
questions.answer_form: a single verdict naming which of the two it requires
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the 'tense is the prior generation's' rule: a layer that stored a tile keeps its fixed declarations (fill included) through the very commit that empties it, so a commit cannot use the empty layer's re-declaration freedom on itself in the same commit — an exception stated explicitly to forestall exactly this reading.

questions.question: A layer is interleaved, rank 2 with dimensions (y, x), extents (1200, 2000) and tile extents (300, 250). It declares a slab with run length S = 5 (and some valid A_slab). At what disk ordinal does slab run index 2 (0-based) begin?
questions.answer_form: a single integer (disk ordinal)
questions.why_it_matters: Requires computing the grid counts and spatial-tile count from §11.2, then applying §16.2's per-block run-partition rule (run r starts at block_start + r*S) to a case with different numbers from the document's own worked slab example, so the answer cannot be transcribed from an example.

questions.question: An interleaved layer has two channels in declared order: `x` (float32) and `y` (uint8); codec 1 (none); filter 2 (byte-shuffle). One tile has exactly two sample positions. Position 0: x = 0x01020304, y = 0xAA. Position 1: x = 0x05060708, y = 0xBB. Give the tile's stored bytes as a single space-separated hex string.
questions.answer_form: uppercase hex bytes, space-separated (e.g. "04 08 03 ...")
questions.why_it_matters: Requires combining the interleaved byte-layout arithmetic (sample stride Q, little-endian channel encoding, §14.2) with the byte-shuffle filter's group/stride transform (§17.3) and then codec 1's 'stored bytes equal filtered image verbatim' rule (§17.2) on values not given anywhere in the document.

questions.question: A layer is planar with channel count C = 3, and its declared geometry gives a spatial-tile count N = 70,000. What is the layer's entry_count, and what is the exact byte length of its tile-index region (entry array plus segment CRC array)?
questions.answer_form: two integers: entry_count, then region length in bytes
questions.why_it_matters: Combines the planar addressed-tile-count rule (C*N, §11.2) with the index-region size formula entry_count*20 + ceil(entry_count/2^16)*4 (§7.4/§15.1), including a non-trivial ceiling-division segment count, on numbers not worked as an example in the document.

questions.question: A planar layer has two channels: channel `a` (float64) whose per-tile decoded plane is 2,400,000,000 bytes, and channel `b` (uint8) whose per-tile decoded plane is 300,000,000 bytes. May a conforming writer declare codec 4 (lz4) for this layer?
questions.answer_form: a single yes/no verdict
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the prose quantifier 'in a planar layer each channel's plane carries its own decoded size, and the largest governs' against the 0x7E000000-byte lz4 cap: channel a alone exceeds the cap even though channel b does not, so the layer-wide codec declaration is barred — a rule easy to lose if 'largest governs' is dropped or softened.

questions.question: During a region read spanning several tiles of one layer, the index-chain verification (segment CRC) for a later tile fails after the reader has already returned some earlier tiles' values to the caller under successfully verified entries. (a) Are those already-returned values retroactively invalidated? (b) What is the disposition of the request's remaining, not-yet-served entries from that same layer?
questions.answer_form: two verdicts, e.g. "(a) no; (b) barred (reject-layer)"
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the 'prospective, not retroactive' character of reject-layer stated in §2.4 and applied concretely in §19.4's tile-read algorithm's step 8 — a subtlety that a reworded 'affected layer is unusable' clause could easily erase.

questions.question: A stored top-level record's flags carry MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 and PRESERVE_ON_EDIT = 0 — a combination no conforming writer emits. (a) Which conformance class is obliged to detect this as a file-conformance violation, reader or verifier? (b) Independent of that detection, what value must any reader or updater treat the record's PRESERVE_ON_EDIT bit as, when deciding whether the record may ever be dropped?
questions.answer_form: an actor name, then a bit value (0 or 1)
questions.why_it_matters: Combines two halves of one rule that a careless rewording could collapse into one: detection of the writer defect is assigned to the verifier alone, while every reader/updater must nonetheless treat the bit as 1 ('never silently deletable') regardless of whether anyone detects the defect.

questions.question: A rewriter is regenerating a layer's tile-index region (because some of the layer's stored extents relocated) and, while classifying entries, meets one that §15.3 classifies reject-tile on a structural ground (for example: offset = sentinel, length != sentinel). Name the rewriter's two possible dispositions for this situation, and state which one is the only way this rewrite can still reclaim that layer's slack.
questions.answer_form: two named dispositions, then which one reclaims slack
questions.why_it_matters: Combines the structural-entry classification of §15.3 (which gives the entry no stored extent to re-point) with §20.5's rewriter rule that such an entry forces a choice between dropping the layer or refusing outright — and only dropping actually completes a rewrite that reclaims anything.

questions.question: File X's trailer has a valid magic and a valid magic-adjacent length gate but its CRC-32C at bytes [60,64) does not match the CRC-32C of trailer bytes [0,60). File Y's trailer has a correct CRC but dir_offset = 10. For each file, name the single register row (an F-number) it is recorded against.
questions.answer_form: two row labels, one per file, e.g. "X: F14; Y: F9"
questions.why_it_matters: Applies the trailer-validation rules of §6.2 to two concrete single-defect cases and requires picking the correct row out of several superficially similar trailer-gate rows in the register.

questions.question: A verifier examines a file and establishes that layer C fails its index CRC (a reject-layer finding), but — having elected to stop at the first violation it finds — never enumerates layers D and E's claimants. (a) How must it report layers D and E? (b) Does that report constitute a finding that D and E are undamaged?
questions.answer_form: a report label, then a yes/no verdict
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the quantifier-laden distinction that 'unexamined' is neither a verdict nor 'cannot establish,' and explicitly is not a finding that the unexamined scope is clean — a nuance a looser paraphrase ('the verifier didn't check them') would erase.

questions.question: A layer is declared planar, rank 3, with a single channel of sample type float64 (element size 8 bytes). Its three dimensions each have extent equal to their own tile extent: 1024, 1024, and 256 (so the layer addresses exactly one tile). The layer declares codec 4 (lz4). Compute this channel's decoded tile size in bytes, and state whether declaring codec 4 on this layer is conforming or a validity error. If it is a validity error, name the outcome class and the owning scope it falls at.
questions.sections: §11.2 (grid/sample-position arithmetic), §14.2 (planar decoded size P·Bᶜ), §17.2 (R-COD-07, the lz4 decoded-size cap)
questions.answer_form: An integer (the decoded size in bytes), plus either 'conforming' or 'validity error' together with the outcome-class name (e.g. reject-layer) and owning scope (layer).
questions.why_it_matters: Tests whether the cap on lz4's declared decoded size is preserved as an exact numeric threshold (0x7E000000) that must be checked against a value derived by combining the layer's geometry formula with its per-type element size — a rewording that drops or fuzzes either the formula or the exact cap loses this.

questions.question: A remote reader opens a 10,000-byte TARN file by issuing a single speculative suffix-range request for the final 300 bytes of the file (byte offsets [9700, 10000)), and uses containment to decide whether a second request is needed. Does this reader's open leave the front signature block (bytes [0, 16)) resident? Per the document's rule, is this reader required to verify the front signature block by byte equality before other processing, or may it defer or omit that check?
questions.sections: §6.1 (R-CNT-04, the residency test for the front signature block), §6.4 (remote open accounting)
questions.answer_form: Two verdicts: (a) 'resident' or 'not resident'; (b) 'MUST verify' or 'MAY defer or omit'.
questions.why_it_matters: The residency carve-out is stated entirely in prose ('a reader that would have to issue a further range request... MAY defer or omit'); a summary that turns this into a flat requirement (or a flat exemption) would be caught by a concrete window that plainly excludes offset 0.

questions.question: A layer record declares index_encoding = 1 and entry_count = 1, with its extent slot's extent_length field set to 40. Applying the document's formula for the tile-index region's byte size under index_encoding 1, is extent_length = 40 correct for this entry_count? If not, state the correct extent_length value, and name the register row this mismatch corresponds to.
questions.sections: §7.4 (the index_encoding-1 extent_length formula, R-CNT-17), §21.3 (register row L22)
questions.answer_form: 'Yes' or 'No', then (if No) an integer giving the correct extent_length, and a row label such as L22.
questions.why_it_matters: The formula includes a ceiling term (⌈entry_count / 2¹⁶⌉ × 4) that is easy to drop or miscompute at entry_count = 1 specifically, since the ceiling of a fraction less than 1 is still 1, not 0 — a natural place for a rewording or a careless implementer to diverge.

questions.question: A layer is interleaved, rank 2, with dimensions declared in this order: dimension 'y' (extent 500, tile extent 128), then dimension 'x' (extent 500, tile extent 128). It has two channels declared in this order: channel 'a' (type int16), then channel 'b' (type uint8). Using linearization 1 (row-major, the only value this format major defines for writers), compute the byte offset — within the decoded tile image of the tile containing coordinate (y, x) = (130, 260) — at which channel 'b's value for that coordinate begins.
questions.sections: §11.2 (grid counts), §11.4 (tile/in-tile ordinals under linearization 1), §14.2 (interleaved byte-offset formula)
questions.answer_form: A single non-negative integer byte offset.
questions.why_it_matters: This chains three separate formulas (grid division, in-tile ordinal, interleaved byte offset with per-channel in-sample offset) end to end; getting any one link wrong — declared dimension order, which dimension varies fastest, or channel stride — changes the final byte a reader would fetch, which is exactly the kind of divergence that produces disagreeing implementations.

questions.question: A layer has two dimensions with extents (7, 7) and tile extents (5, 5), and one channel of type uint16 with declared fill value 0xBEEF. Consider the tile at tile coordinates (1, 1) (the high-edge tile along both axes). How many of that tile's sample positions are padding positions (i.e., lie outside the layer's extents)? For any one such padding position, what are the exact two stored bytes, in order, that a conforming stored tile must encode there for this channel (give them as upper-case hex byte pairs)?
questions.sections: §11.2-§11.3 (grid arithmetic and padding positions), §13.1 (fill field, little-endian encoding), §14.5 (R-SER-05, padding content fixed to fill)
questions.answer_form: An integer count of padding positions, plus two upper-case hex bytes in stored order (e.g. 'EF BE').
questions.why_it_matters: Combines a geometry computation (how many of 25 positions in a 5x5 edge tile are real vs. padding, given extent 7) with the prose rule that padding content is not arbitrary but is fixed, byte-for-byte, to the channel's recorded fill in its stored little-endian form — a rewording that treats padding as unconstrained content would fail this outright.

questions.question: A planar layer has three channels declared in this order: 'r' (uint8, fill 10), 'g' (uint8, fill 20), 'b' (uint8, fill 30). At one particular spatial tile ordinal, the tile for channel 'r' is stored and decodes to value 200 at a given in-tile position, the tile for channel 'g' at that same spatial ordinal is the sentinel (unstored), and the tile for channel 'b' is stored and decodes to value 5 at that position. What are the three channel values of the sample at that coordinate, in declared channel order (r, g, b)?
questions.sections: §3.2 (planar per-channel storedness independence), §13.3 (R-TYP-08, unstored tiles read as fill)
questions.answer_form: An ordered list/tuple of three integers, e.g. '(200, 20, 5)'.
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the specific planar rule that a single sample's channels can independently mix decoded and fill values — a rewording that treated storedness as a per-sample (rather than per-tile-per-channel) property would answer this differently.

questions.question: A layer is planar with a bool channel whose tile is a packed boolean plane (i.e., its decoded image is bit-packed per §14.3, not a byte-per-value plane). If filter 2 (byte-shuffle) is declared for this layer, what is the byte-shuffle stride s applied to this channel's packed plane, and what is the practical effect of applying filter 2 at that stride on the plane's stored bytes?
questions.sections: §14.3 (packed boolean planes), §17.3 (R-COD-10, byte-shuffle stride rule and its packed-bool-plane carve-out)
questions.answer_form: An integer stride value, plus a short phrase describing the effect (e.g. 'identity — the bytes are unchanged').
questions.why_it_matters: The general byte-shuffle stride rule (element size for planar, sample stride Q for interleaved) is explicitly overridden for packed boolean planes, where stride is fixed at 1 and the filter becomes a no-op; a summary that applies the general formula uniformly, without the carve-out, gets this case wrong.

questions.question: A verifier is checking a file. During its coverage walk, it reaches a layer whose stored-tile decode it declines purely on resource grounds (invoking the document's resource-limit provision), and, apart from that decline, it establishes no violation anywhere else in the file. What single verdict word does the verifier report for the file as a whole — one of: conforming, nonconforming, cannot establish? And when it reports the file's slack-byte total, must that total be reported as complete or as partial?
questions.sections: §2.3 (R-CNF-11, verifier verdicts), §21.9 (R-ERR-04, resource declines), §5.2/§9.7 (R-CNT-21, R-LIF-08, slack totals)
questions.answer_form: One verdict word, plus 'complete' or 'partial'.
questions.why_it_matters: Combines the rule that a resource decline is not itself a finding of nonconformance (so the verdict is 'cannot establish', not 'nonconforming') with the separate rule that an incomplete coverage walk forces the slack total to be reported as a partial upper bound rather than an exact figure — two related but distinct exceptions that a rewording could easily collapse into one or drop.

questions.question: A layer's tile-index entry has offset = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF (the sentinel value) and length = 100 (not the sentinel value), with crc = 0. Per the document's entry-classification table, what outcome class applies to this entry (name it exactly)? Is this classification one the document calls 'structural', or does it instead leave the entry 'well-formed'? Consequently, does this entry contribute a claimant to a verifier's coverage-walk enumeration, or do the bytes it nominally addresses fall to slack?
questions.sections: §15.3 (entry-validity table, R-IDX-03), §9.7/§5.2 (R-LIF-08, coverage-walk consequence of a structurally-classified entry)
questions.answer_form: The outcome-class name (e.g. 'reject-tile'), then 'structural' or 'well-formed', then 'contributes a claimant' or 'falls to slack'.
questions.why_it_matters: This ties a specific row of the entry-validity table to a downstream, cross-referenced consequence for coverage/slack accounting stated in a different section — a rewording that keeps the table row but loses the cross-reference would answer the classification correctly but the coverage-walk question wrongly.

questions.question: A layer stored at least one tile in the generation an appender's commit supersedes. That layer is planar with channels declared in order (p, q, r). The commit's only change to this layer is to insert a new channel 's' into the channel list between 'q' and 'r' — that is, not at the end of the list. Is this change one an appender may make to this layer within a single commit, or does achieving it require treating the result as a new layer (under a different name) or performing a whole-file rewrite?
questions.sections: §20.3 step 4 (the closed list of permitted vs. fixed declarations for a layer that stored a tile in the superseded generation)
questions.answer_form: One of: 'permitted as an appender commit' or 'not permitted — requires a new layer or a rewrite'.
questions.why_it_matters: The document permits extending or shortening a planar channel list only at its end; inserting a channel anywhere else is explicitly listed among the changes that are rewrites even though the same file might survive them in place — a carve-out easy to lose in summary as 'channel lists can be edited'.

questions.question: A rewriter performs pure compaction on a file: every stored tile's bytes, every index entry's offset/length/crc, and every retained record's content are carried forward completely unchanged from the input, with only the byte placement of structures in the output differing from the input. True or false: this rewriter is permitted to reuse the input file's file_id value for its output trailer, since the output's decoded content is byte-for-byte identical to the input's.
questions.sections: §20.5 (R-WRT-06, mandatory fresh file_id on any rewrite), §9.3 (R-LIF-03, the (file_id, range) cache-soundness contract)
questions.answer_form: 'True' or 'False'.
questions.why_it_matters: The document is explicit that even a content-identical compaction MUST mint a fresh file_id, because relocation changes what bytes occupy a given range and reusing the identifier would break the cache-soundness contract — a plausible but wrong reading is that byte-identical content licenses reusing the identifier.

questions.question: A file's directory region, taken as a byte sequence, has a final 4 bytes that correctly equal the CRC-32C of the preceding dir_length − 4 bytes. However, this same file's trailer declares version_major = 2, a major value the reader does not implement (version_major is not 0). Following the document's mandated order for validating a file's trailer and its stated open-algorithm step ordering, does a conforming reader ever reach the point of fetching and verifying this directory region's CRC for this file? Answer yes or no, and name the step or rule at which the reader's processing stops.
questions.sections: §6.2 (R-CNT-06, the mandated trailer-validation order), §6.3 (R-CNT-07, the version gate), §19.1 (the open algorithm's step ordering)
questions.answer_form: 'Yes' or 'No', plus the name of the stopping step/rule (e.g. 'the version gate, during trailer validation, before the directory step').
questions.why_it_matters: Tests whether the strict, explicitly ordered sequence of trailer gates (magic, CRC, version, then remaining field gates) — which precedes the directory fetch entirely — survives a rewording; a version reordering that let readers fetch the directory before or independent of the version gate would change this answer.

questions.question: A layer declares a slab with run length S = 8, and one particular run covers disk ordinals [40, 48). Ordinal 42's tile-index entry has length = 0 (a non-sentinel entry), which the document's entry-validity table classifies on a structural ground. Ordinal 44's entry is a valid sentinel. Every other ordinal in the run (40, 41, 43, 45, 46, 47) has a normal, well-formed, stored entry. Does ordinal 42's structurally-invalid entry, by itself, cause this run to fail the slab run-continuity invariant that a verifier checks?
questions.sections: §16.2 (R-SLB-03, slab run continuity and its transparency carve-out for sentinels and structurally-rejected entries)
questions.answer_form: 'Yes' or 'No'.
questions.why_it_matters: The document states that both sentinel entries and entries classified reject-tile on a structural ground are 'transparent' to run continuity — they neither occupy bytes nor break packing — while an entry that only fails its stored-bytes CRC is not transparent. A rewording that treats every invalid entry the same way would answer this incorrectly.

questions.question: An appender's commit supersedes exactly one stored tile belonging to a layer whose tile index has more than one CRC segment (i.e., entry_count exceeds 65,536). The superseded tile's index entry lies in segment 2 of that index; segment 0 is untouched by this commit — none of its entries change value or position — but because the commit changes the layer's stored-tile set, the whole tile-index region (all segments, including segment 0) is re-emitted in the new generation, with segment 0's entries copied forward byte-identically. Per the document's stated verification-depth rule for updaters, must the appender verify segment 0's index chain (its crc_of_crc_array cross-check and its own segment CRC) before it re-emits segment 0's entries in the new tile-index region?
questions.sections: §20.3 (R-WRT-03, an updater's verification-depth-follows-reliance rule, 'the §19.4 index chain for every segment whose entries the commit reuses')
questions.answer_form: 'Yes' or 'No'.
questions.why_it_matters: The verification-depth rule is stated over 'every segment whose entries the commit reuses' — a phrase that, read carefully, reaches every segment copied forward during a full re-emission, not merely the segment containing the touched entry. A rewording that narrowed this to 'the segment being modified' would answer differently.

questions.question: Among the eight numeric identifier spaces the document's registry section tabulates (record type, channel layout, linearization, sample type, codec, filter, index encoding, metadata encoding), exactly one is defined with no experimental range at all. Name that space. Given that fact, if a writer's channel layout field held the value 200, would a reader classify 200 as falling in that space's experimental range, or in its reserved range?
questions.sections: §10.2 (the numeric-identifier-space table and its accompanying prose, R-EXT-02)
questions.answer_form: The exact name of the identifier space (e.g. 'channel layout'), plus 'experimental' or 'reserved'.
questions.why_it_matters: This is a quantifier stated once in prose ('one space carries no experimental range... 3 through 255 staying reserved') rather than something visible from the table's shape alone unless the reader also parses the prose explaining why; a rewording that silently gave channel layout an experimental range, or moved the exception to a different space, would be caught here.

answers.decisive_quote: Sentinel tiles are transparent to run continuity ... So are the entries §15.3 classifies reject-tile on a *structural* ground: they address no usable extent, and the run's stored tiles close over them.
answers.reasoning: Ordinal 42's length=0 non-sentinel entry is classified *structural* by §15.3, and [R-SLB-03] explicitly makes structural entries transparent to run continuity exactly like sentinels (ordinal 44). With every other ordinal in the run well-formed and stored, the run-continuity invariant is not, by itself, broken by ordinal 42.

answers.decisive_quote: the §19.4 index chain for every segment whose entries the commit reuses (`[R-IDX-04]`). Structures the commit neither modifies nor relies on impose no further obligation.
answers.reasoning: Segment 0's entries are reused (copied forward byte-identically into the re-emitted tile-index region), so under [R-WRT-03]'s reliance principle the appender must verify segment 0's index chain — crc_of_crc_array cross-check and the segment's own CRC — before re-emitting it, even though none of segment 0's entries change value or position.

answers.decisive_quote: One space carries no experimental range: channel layout, whose `u8` field is too narrow to spare one, 3 through 255 staying reserved to this specification.
answers.reasoning: The §10.2 table shows channel layout as Assigned {1,2}, Reserved {3-255}, Experimental: none — the only one of the eight spaces with no experimental range. A value of 200 falls in 3-255, which is entirely reserved (there is no experimental sub-range to compete for it).

probe_answers.answer: Baseline: 2 requests. (1) A suffix fetch of the final 64 bytes -- byte range [F-64,F) = [4032,4096) once F is known -- whose response also discloses the complete length (F=4096), satisfying open-steps 1 and 2 together. (2) [dir_offset, dir_offset+dir_length), read out of the now-validated trailer. Total bytes fetched = 64 + dir_length; dir_length is not given by the probe, so no single integer total can be stated. The second range's start is bound by dir_offset and its length by dir_length, both trailer fields, usable only after the trailer CRC covering them has verified. The document explicitly licenses an alternative 1-request strategy (a speculative suffix fetch plus containment), since request count is stated to be 'a theory of operation, not a budget' -- so the exact number of requests is an implementation choice, not fixed by conformance; I give the document's own stated baseline as the canonical answer.

probe_answers.answer: Top-level record of an unimplemented type carrying MU=1: reject-file ([R-CNT-15]) -- the whole file becomes unusable. As a sub-record of the same type nested inside a layer record: reject-layer only ([R-CNT-18]); the document is explicit that 'where the file is otherwise conforming a reader MUST NOT reject the file for it,' so every other layer and every other top-level record remain fully usable. findings.title: No outcome class defined for a reader lacking a mandatory (core) codec or filter
findings.detail: Every assigned codec (1-4) and filter (1-2) value is core: a conforming reader MUST implement all of them (R-CNF-03, restated at R-COD-03/R-COD-09). For the adjacent, well-specified cases the document is explicit: an invalid/reserved/experimental codec or filter value is reject-layer (L43/L45); a verifier unable to execute a codec reports 'cannot establish' (R-COD-11); and exactly two capability refusals are named as conforming-file-but-refused cases in §21.6's closing paragraph (an unimplemented format major, and an unimplemented top-level MU=1 record type). For a reader (not a verifier) lacking an assigned, core codec/filter it can't execute, R-COD-11's only statement is that such software 'is not a conforming reader' -- it disqualifies the implementation from the conformance class rather than prescribing any behavior, and is not reached by R-ERR-04's resource-decline licence (which governs §21.9's guarantee table) or by either of the two named capability refusals. An implementer building software that knowingly supports fewer than all four codecs has no textual answer for what a spec-following degraded behavior looks like here -- the document simply defines the question out of existence for conforming software. An implementer reading a different edition whose §17.4/§21.9 wording differs slightly (e.g. extending R-ERR-04's licence to cover this ground, or extending R-COD-11's 'cannot establish' framing to readers) would answer probe R3 differently.
findings.quotation_a: software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: A conforming reader is required, unconditionally, to implement all four codecs and both filters (R-CNF-03), so this scenario is definitionally impossible for any implementation the specification's acceptance/rejection obligations apply to. Resolving the gap would only add guidance for software that has already left the conformance class by the document's own terms; it changes no accept/reject/emit boundary for a conforming file or a conforming reader.

The open path for a remote reader with disclosed range-response lengths is exactly two requests - a suffix fetch of the final 64 bytes (which also discloses the transport-authoritative file size F, merging the open algorithm's steps 1-2) and a fetch of [dir_offset, dir_offset+dir_length) - with dir_offset/dir_length themselves bounded by trailer fields validated (per the document's own ordered-validation and verify-before-acting rules) before being used to form that second range. Validation timing splits cleanly into four tiers (open, layer access, tile use, extent use), each decidable from bytes already in hand at that tier with the sole exception of tile use, which is the first tier costing further I/O. The tile-read algorithm bottoms out in fully specified byte-offset arithmetic for both planar and interleaved layouts, which I exercised on a constructed example (interleaved, two 2-D dimensions with distinct extents/tile-extents, two channels of different sizes) and got a disk ordinal of 4 and a channel-b byte offset of 17, cross-checked against the neighboring channel's offset for consistency. Two implementations, both accepting every conforming file within the guaranteed limits and rejecting every register-condemned file, can diverge on such a file: one serves every reference-array byte for the zstd-coded layer, another refuses the whole file, another refuses only that layer, and another attempts a partial decode - the document licenses and forbids none of these explicitly, because by R-CNF-03's own terms the implementation lacking zstd is not 'a conforming reader' the moment it lacks it, so no requirement written for conforming readers binds it at all.

probe_answers.answer: Not permitted as an appender operation: fill is one of the fixed declarations bound to a layer for as long as it stores a tile, and a commit MUST NOT change it -- 'not an appender's operation at all.' The document names two operations instead: (1) drop the layer and add a new one (same or different name) with the new fill declared fresh; (2) a whole-file rewrite that re-declares the layer under a fresh file_id. Whether the resulting file (if such a forbidden commit were made anyway) is nonconforming is conditional: this specific bar is one of three rules the document expressly says binds writer conduct rather than file conformance, so the violation alone does not make the file nonconforming and no register row records it directly -- but if the affected tile has any padding position (or, for a packed bool plane, pad bits), the tile's already-stored bytes still encode the old fill while the newly-declared fill now governs what padding must encode, which IS a detectable, verifier-caught violation (T4, and T5 for pad bits). If the tile has no padding at all, no such consequence is stated, and the resulting file could remain byte-conforming despite the writer-conduct violation.

This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself... a file such a commit leaves can be nonconforming on its own terms, as the paragraph below sets out.

probe_answers.answer: The next reader, on the default open path, finds no valid trailer in the file's final 64 bytes (the pad+trailer from this commit's step 5 were never made durable) and MUST report the file torn or invalid, and MUST NOT scan backward. As raw bytes at this instant, the file is not a conforming file (it fails the trailer gates at its own physical end). The next appender does not simply resume: it must first attempt to establish F by validating the trailer at the physical end; on failure it MUST NOT append, and must instead run the deliberate recovery scan of §9.6 -- probing backward at 64-aligned offsets for the trailer magic, accepting a candidate only if its CRC verifies and committed_file_length = offset+64, taking the nearest-to-end surviving candidate (which is the prior generation's trailer, untouched because committed bytes below the old F are immutable), re-verifying the whole file up to that point, and truncating to it -- before resuming any further commit from that recovered F.
probe_answers.citations: `[R-LIF-05]` (default read path, torn/no-scan-back); §9.4 (`[R-LIF-04]`, no append on torn file, recovery is deliberate and separate); §9.6 (`[R-LIF-06]`, the recovery scan and re-verification procedure); §9.1 (`[R-LIF-01]`, committed-prefix immutability).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: The default read path is trailer-at-end-or-fail: a reader that finds no valid trailer in the final 64 bytes MUST report the file torn or invalid and MUST NOT scan backward... If that validation fails, the file is torn: the writer MUST NOT append, and locating the last committed state is the deliberate recovery operation of §9.6 -- never an implicit step of opening for append.

probe_answers.answer: An 'unimplemented sample type' must be a reserved or experimental type value (all 13 assigned types are core and mandatory for every conforming reader), which is a layer-scope validity error decidable from the declared type field alone, with no decode required. Because a rewriter must fully validate every retained layer's record before emitting anything of it, it detects this violation before it ever reaches the tiles -- it never gets to 'carry forward tiles it cannot decode' as a distinct step. For stored tiles generally, what a rewriter must verify is checksum-only: the index chain (crc_of_crc_array, segment CRC) and each stored tile's own entry crc against its stored bytes -- never a decode. When any such check fails (the type-value check, or a tile's crc), the rewriter has detected a violation and MUST NOT emit a file carrying it; since the layer record's own flags are fixed by the registry at MU=0/PE=0, dropping the whole layer is licensed (SHOULD report the loss), and refusing to rewrite the whole file is the only other option. It may NOT instead re-create the layer: re-creation requires decoding the layer's content as a reader and writing it fresh as a creator, which is exactly what is unavailable here (an unimplemented type, or corrupted bytes in the crc-failure reading).

The only way a channel's type can be one the rewriter 'cannot decode' is an out-of-range value (outside 1-13), which is not a decode failure but a structural, layer-scope violation (L34) caught at mandatory layer-access validation, before any tile is examined. Under the general chain-of-reliance rule regardless: the rewriter must verify the checksum chain (open, layer record, full index chain, and each copied extent's own checksum, including every stored tile's entry crc) before emitting anything, whether or not it can decode the content. If any such check fails, its only two disposals are to drop the whole layer (licensed since the layer record is PE=0, SHOULD report the loss) or refuse to rewrite the file entirely — there is no per-tile partial remedy in a rewrite. It may re-create the layer only if it can decode it as a reader; by the scenario's premise it cannot, so re-creation is unavailable to it.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "This specification defines exactly thirteen sample types, all core: a conforming reader MUST decode every one of them, and none is skippable."

probe_answers.answer: Three verdicts: conforming, nonconforming, cannot establish. (Plus a non-verdict report marker, 'unexamined', which the document explicitly says is neither a verdict nor 'cannot establish'.) One triggering condition each: conforming - the verifier completes its walk, verifies every checksum, decodes every tile, and establishes no violation and no unchecked requirement anywhere. nonconforming - the verifier establishes any single violation (e.g. a trailer-CRC mismatch, F14), which takes priority 'however many requirements it was unable to check.' cannot establish - the verifier establishes no violation anywhere but is unable to check some requirement on a capability/resource ground (e.g. it cannot execute a layer's declared codec, R-COD-11).
probe_answers.citations: §2.3 R-CNF-11 (verdict definitions and priority rule); §19.2's note on 'unexamined'
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "A verifier reports one of three verdicts: conforming, nonconforming, or cannot establish" ... "Unexamined is neither a verdict nor cannot establish—it constrains the report, not the verdict."

probe_answers.answer: Branches on the type's numeric range, which the probe does not state. Reserved range (0x0003-0x7FFF): emitting the type with MU=1 is itself violation F35 (an instance of F36); detector reader, at open; a verifier reports NONCONFORMING. Experimental range (>=0x8000): not a violation at all (§21.6); the reader/verifier must still reject on capability grounds (R-CNT-15), and R-CNF-11 lists exactly this pattern as a cannot-establish ground; if no other violation exists, the verdict is CANNOT ESTABLISH.
probe_answers.citations: §2.2/§10.2 (value-space ranges); §21.2 F35/F36, R-CNT-15; §21.6 closing paragraph; §2.3 R-CNF-11
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "a reserved-range type carrying MU = 1 is itself a violation" (R-CNF-03) vs. "R-CNT-15 obliges the reader to reject, and R-CNF-02 makes the file conforming all the same" (§21.6), listed by R-CNF-11 as a cannot-establish ground: "when a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement (§21.6)".

probe_answers.answer: Verdict: CANNOT ESTABLISH, provided the verifier establishes no other violation in the file (otherwise NONCONFORMING takes priority regardless). The report must name the requirement it could not check (§14's decoded-content obligations, R-SER-05/R-SER-08, and the exact-size/framing checks that require decoding) and the ground (inability to execute that layer's declared codec/filter), per R-CNF-11's per-requirement reporting duty. Caveat the document itself draws: this scenario is only the behavior of a fully-conforming verifier when the codec value is one of the four assigned/core values (1-4); if the declared codec value is itself reserved or experimental, that is independently register row L43 (reject-layer, detector reader, at layer access) with no execution needed at all, making the file NONCONFORMING on that ground alone.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "A verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter cannot establish that layer's conformance and MUST NOT certify the file... it fixes the file's verdict as cannot establish only where the verifier established no violation elsewhere."

probe_answers.answer: The verifier cannot see it as such: the coverage walk examines only the live generation and never reconstructs or compares against prior generations (§9.7), and the prohibition itself is a writer-conduct rule explicitly declared to state 'no condition a file can exhibit' and to carry no register row (§20.3 step 4, citing R-ERR-01/R-CNF-02). Whether any verdict follows at all depends on which fixed declaration changed: changes affecting decoded size, padding/pad-bit content, boolean-byte domain, or codec/filter framing incidentally surface as ordinary tile-scope violations (T3/T14/T21/T22, T4/T5/T2, or T17/T24/T25 respectively) and DO make the file NONCONFORMING - but only because of that incidental byte mismatch, never because 'a fixed declaration changed.' Any other fixed-declaration change (e.g. a name, or one whose old and new decoded images coincide) leaves no trace at all, and the verdict is unaffected (CONFORMING if nothing else is wrong).
probe_answers.citations: §9.7 (R-LIF-08, no history reconstruction); §20.3 step 4 (the fixed-declaration bar and its 'no condition a file can exhibit' classification); §21.7 R-ERR-01
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "Nothing here enumerates prior commits. A verifier certifies what a reader can reach and counts what it cannot... does not depend on reconstructing the file's history." / "no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself... the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit" / "but for a stored tile's decoded size, a padding position or pad bit, or a boolean byte the register witnesses (T3, T14, T21, T22, T4, T5, T2) and a decode that fails outright, or a codec's framing check that precedes it, under a changed codec or filter (T17, T24, T25), no check any actor owes able to see it".

probe_answers.answer: The verifier treats the MU=1/PE=0 combination as a validity error at the record's own governing scope, which is verifier-detected (ordinary readers/updaters instead just resolve the flag combination to PE=1 and proceed unchanged, per R-CNT-12). At file scope (a non-layer top-level record): register row F25, detector verifier, detected at certification, outcome reject-file. At layer scope (a layer record, or one of its sub-records): register row L46, detector verifier, detected at certification, outcome reject-layer. Either way the file becomes nonconforming even though no reader's own served behavior changes.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "a verifier MUST treat a nonzero reserved flag bit or the MU = 1 with PE = 0 combination as a validity error at the record's governing scope" (R-CNT-12); "R-CNT-12's reading of MU = 1 with PE = 0 as PE = 1 (F25, L46) resolves a flag and returns no data" (§21.1)

findings.location_a: §2.3 (R-CNF-11), the cannot-establish trigger list; and §21.6's closing paragraph on the same structural pattern
findings.title: A file can be byte-predicate-conforming yet no verifier may ever certify it 'conforming'
findings.detail: R-CNF-11 unconditionally lists 'a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement (§21.6)' as a cannot-establish ground. §21.6, discussing the identical pattern (an experimental-range top-level record type carrying MU=1), states the file 'carries no violation at all' — i.e. it is a conforming file under the specification's own byte predicate. Since experimental values are by definition private and collision-unprotected (§10.3), no general verifier implements them all, so for this entire class of genuinely conforming files, an implementer following R-CNF-11 to the letter must never emit the verdict 'conforming' — only 'cannot establish' (or 'nonconforming' if something else is also wrong). An implementer who instead reasons from §21.6 alone ('no violation at all' -> report conforming) would violate R-CNF-11's explicit bar on certifying a file it cannot fully check.

findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: It fixes, for an entire structural family of inputs (top-level experimental-range MU=1 records), that a conforming verifier implementation may never emit the byte-level verdict 'conforming' no matter how completely it checks everything else in the file — a concrete, permanent constraint on what output such an implementation may ever produce for that input class.

A verifier or vector author encountering some other pair of rows with this relationship (if one exists elsewhere in the register) has no closed list to consult and must re-derive the property, which is an operational hazard for building a complete, correctly-attributed conformance corpus (R-VEC-02/R-VEC-03) even though it changes no accepted or rejected byte.

probe_answers.answer: Three verdicts: conforming (every requirement checked, none violated); nonconforming (at least one violation established -- takes priority over any number of unchecked requirements); cannot establish (no violation established, but some requirement was one the verifier could not check on a capability or resource ground -- e.g. an unimplemented format major, an unimplemented MU=1 record type, an inexecutable codec/filter, a resource-declined layer/tile/document decode). 'Unexamined' (used when a verifier stops at the first violation found) and the mandatory per-requirement capability/resource report are explicitly NOT part of this three-way vocabulary -- they constrain the report, not the verdict.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: A verifier reports one of three verdicts: conforming, nonconforming, or cannot establish ... Cannot establish is not a finding that the file is nonconforming ... An established violation takes priority ... Unexamined is neither a verdict nor cannot establish.

probe_answers.answer: Depends on the type's numeric range, which the document fully determines once known. Reserved range (0x0003-0x7FFF): emitting the type at all is already the violation F36, and MU=1 on it is the further violation F35 -- verdict NONCONFORMING; reader still reject-files per R-CNT-15. Experimental range (>=0x8000): not a violation at all (one of §21.6's two 'conforming files a reader nevertheless refuses'; R-CNF-02 makes the file conforming despite the mandatory reject-file); verdict is CANNOT ESTABLISH (§2.3 lists 'a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND=1 with a type it does not implement' as a cannot-establish ground), since the verifier has established no violation but cannot check what that record governs. The requirement fixing the reader-visible reject-file action in both cases is R-CNT-15.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: an experimental-range top-level record type carrying MU = 1 (§10.2, §10.3): [R-CNT-15] obliges the reader to reject, and [R-CNF-02] makes the file conforming all the same.

probe_answers.answer: Verdict: CANNOT ESTABLISH for the whole file, provided the verifier established no violation elsewhere (R-CNF-11's priority rule). For a genuinely conforming verifier this can only arise at a reserved/experimental codec or filter value, which is already an independent, immediately-checkable L43/L45 violation (no decode needed) -- in that case the verdict is actually NONCONFORMING via L43/L45, established before execution is even attempted. The report for that layer names the specific unchecked decoded-content requirement(s) (R-SER-05 padding/fill, R-SER-08 bool bytes, R-SER-07 decoded-size-exactness, or the codec-family T-rows) and the ground ('cannot execute codec/filter N', R-COD-11); it does NOT need to make the layer's coverage-walk contribution partial, since enumerating a layer's claimants (extent slot, index checksums, entry crc over stored bytes) never requires executing the codec or filter -- only certifying its decoded content does.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: A verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter cannot establish that layer's conformance and MUST NOT certify the file ... For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core.

probe_answers.answer: No -- the verifier cannot see it as such. §20.3 step 4's bar on changing a fixed declaration of a layer that stored a tile is an explicit writer-conduct rule: 'no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself ... the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit' (R-ERR-01, R-CNF-02). The verifier's certification model examines only the single live generation reachable from the live trailer (§9.7) and has no field or mechanism recording prior generations or commit count at all (§9.3's note), so 'the last commit changed X' is not even a question the format lets a verifier ask. No violation is established by this fact alone, and it is not 'cannot establish' either (that vocabulary covers a known-needed check the verifier lacks capability/resource for; here there is nothing to check against). The one incidental exception: if the new declaration also makes the old stored bytes fail an ordinary, unrelated structural/content check under the new reading (a decoded-size mismatch T3, a fill/padding mismatch T4/T5, a bool-byte violation T2, a decode failure under a changed codec/filter T17/T24/T25), that row fires on its own terms -- but this detects the resulting mismatch, not the re-declaration itself, and the document says explicitly that in general 'no check any actor owes [is] able to see it' (§21.7).
probe_answers.citations: §20.3 step 4 (long paragraph and its Note), §9.3 (third Note), §9.7 (Note), §21.7; `[R-ERR-01]`, `[R-CNF-02]`
probe_answers.decisive_quote: This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself ... Nothing here enumerates prior commits. A verifier certifies what a reader can reach and counts what it cannot ... does not depend on reconstructing the file's history.

probe_answers.answer: Two distinct things happen. (1) Every reader/updater, unconditionally, treats the record as if PE were 1 -- 'never silently deletable' -- regardless of certification. (2) The verifier additionally treats the MU=1/PE=0 combination itself as a validity error at the record's own governing scope: file scope (reject-file, register row F25) if it is a non-layer top-level record, or layer scope (reject-layer, register row L46) if it is a layer record or one of its sub-records. Either way the file's verdict is NONCONFORMING (an established violation); the F25-vs-L46 split determines only how much of the file the finding condemns, following the general owning-scope mapping (file/layer/tile) stated for every structure.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: Writers MUST NOT emit the combination MU = 1 with PE = 0; a reader or updater encountering it MUST treat the record as PE = 1 ... a verifier MUST treat a nonzero reserved flag bit or the MU = 1 with PE = 0 combination as a validity error at the record's governing scope.

findings.title: Codec/filter execution failure (R-COD-11) is not listed among the coverage-walk's own partial-total triggers
findings.detail: §5.2/§9.7 (R-LIF-08, R-CNT-21) enumerate exactly three things that make a verifier's coverage-walk slack total partial: a scope-level rejection blocking enumeration, a layer declined on resource grounds (R-ERR-04), or the verifier stopping at the first violation (R-CNF-11). R-COD-11's 'cannot execute a layer's codec or filter' capability decline is never named in that list. Since a layer's coverage-walk claimants (its extent slot, index-region checksums, and each entry's crc over stored bytes) are all establishable without invoking the codec or filter -- only §14's decoded-content obligations (R-SER-05, R-SER-08) require decoding -- an implementer following only §5.2/§9.7's literal trigger list could reasonably conclude (correctly, I believe, but only by inference) that a verifier stuck on R-COD-11 for one layer still reports an EXACT slack/live-state total for the whole file, even though it cannot certify. An implementer who instead assumed decode-inability must degrade the walk to 'partial' (by analogy with R-ERR-04) would produce a materially different verifier report from one who read the sections as I did.
findings.quotation_a: n/a
findings.quotation_b: Where the walk does not complete — a scope-level rejection blocks enumeration, the verifier declines a layer on resource grounds and so never enumerates its claimants ([R-ERR-04]), or it stops at the first violation ([R-CNF-11]) — the sum is reported as partial
findings.byte_level_rationale: This affects only the verifier's diagnostic report (whether the slack figure is labeled exact or partial) alongside a verdict that is already independently fixed at 'cannot establish' (or 'nonconforming', if the codec value is itself reserved/experimental) by R-COD-11/L43/L45. It does not change which file bytes a conforming writer may emit, nor which files a conforming reader must accept or reject -- only a secondary field of the verifier's own report.

findings.title: A commit that silently violates the fixed-declaration bar is undetectable by the verifier's certification model except by accident
findings.detail: §20.3 step 4 explicitly states that a commit changing a fixed declaration of a layer that stored a tile 'binds the commit as an actor' and carries 'no register row', and §9.7's own Note confirms the verifier's certification model has no access to prior generations at all ('does not depend on reconstructing the file's history'). The document is internally consistent and not contradictory here, but the practical consequence -- that a verifier can and, per the design, sometimes MUST certify a file whose last commit reinterpreted a stored tile's fill, type, codec, or geometry in place, provided the old bytes happen to still parse under the new declaration -- is easy for an implementer to miss, since every other structural change in §20.3-§20.5 has a corresponding register row or explicit non-violation entry, and this is the one place the document says outright that detection is sometimes simply unavailable to any actor.
findings.quotation_a: n/a
findings.quotation_b: This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself, the register enumerating file-conformance violations (§21.1) and the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit (§21.7, [R-ERR-01], [R-CNF-02])
findings.byte_level_rationale: This determines a real accept/reject outcome: given the SAME live-state bytes (a layer whose current declarations happen to still validate structurally against its stored tiles), a conforming verifier MUST certify the file even if that layer's declarations were in fact changed illegitimately across the last commit -- the certification result depends only on whether the current bytes pass every register row, never on the commit history that produced them.

result.summary: The two editions are not a broad readability rewrite in practice: a full line-level diff of the two 300KB files shows they are byte-identical except at exactly six small, surgical edit sites (net line-count delta of 4 lines, cross-checked against the six hunks' own line-count changes). None of the eight probes' cited passages, and none of either walk's own self-reported findings' cited passages, fall inside any of those six sites except one (the F19 register row), so every probe-level agreement between the two reader-implementer walks is a genuine agreement over identical text, not a lucky agreement over diverging text - I checked this explicitly per charter item 2 and found no counterexample. Both walks' shared finding (no outcome class for a reader lacking a mandatory codec, readera-01/readerb-01) traces to text confirmed byte-identical in both editions (Sections 17.2, 17.4, 21.6, 21.9), so it is an EQUIVALENT, pre-existing indeterminacy in the shared source, not a fidelity divergence. Of the six genuine differences: (1) Section 6.3 drops an explicit 'MUST NOT clear them' obligation on an updater handling unknown ignore-lane flag bits - a LOSS with a plausible byte-level effect. (2) Section 20.3's appender-obligation sentence drops 'save where Section 20.4 licenses the drop', turning a conditional prohibition into an unconditional one that now contradicts Section 20.4's own MU=0/PE=0 drop licence within edition B itself - a LOSS, byte-level true. (3) A worked example's arithmetic (32*20+4) is correctly 644 in edition A and wrongly stated as 664 in edition B - a LOSS in a non-normative example, byte-level plausible but not established. (4) Section 20.4's statement of which types the MU=1 re-emission row reaches is inverted in edition B ('reaches only a type the updater does not implement' becomes 'reaches every type, implemented or not'), producing a sentence in edition B that contradicts its own very next clause - flagged as both CONTRADICTION and LOSS, byte-level plausible divergence. (5) Section 20.4 drops an entire sentence stating that an unimplemented critical (MU=1) sub-record blocks a layer from being dropped at all - a clean LOSS of an exception, byte-level true, since an updater built from edition B alone may drop a layer that edition A (and edition B's own MU=1 table row) forbids dropping. (6) Register row F19's Instances cell narrows from 'flags bits 0-15' (edition A, matching its own Condition text) to 'flags bits 0-7' (edition B) - confirming reader B's own finding readerb-02 as a genuine edition-B-only defect (not present in edition A), byte-level false since the governing rule R-CNT-08 is unqualified and identical in both editions. All eight register-table rows and code sections the probes depend on (R1 through R8) were independently verified byte-identical between editions beyond the six hunches, so every probe answer pair is classified EQUIVALENT.

findings.location_a: Section 6.3 (an updater's ignore-lane flag-bit obligations, governing rule [R-CNT-08])
findings.location_b: Section 6.3, same paragraph, same rule tag [R-CNT-08]
findings.title: Edition B drops the explicit 'MUST NOT clear them' obligation for an updater's unknown ignore-lane bits
findings.detail: Edition A imposes three distinct obligations on an updater regarding an ignore-lane bit (bits 16-31) it does not understand: it MUST copy the bit forward, it MUST NOT clear it, and it MUST NOT set any other such bit. Edition B states only the first and third obligations, dropping the middle clause entirely. 'Copy forward' alone does not unambiguously forbid an updater from zeroing a specific bit it considers meaningless while otherwise regenerating the trailer's flags word from the file's overall feature set; the explicit 'MUST NOT clear them' in A is what forecloses that reading. An implementer building strictly from B's text could conclude it is permitted to clear an unknown ignore-lane bit during a rewrite or append, since B states no prohibition against it, whereas an implementer building from A is explicitly barred from doing so.
findings.quotation_a: An updater MUST copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits of its input file, MUST NOT clear them, and MUST NOT set any other: no writer under this text originates an ignore-lane bit...
findings.quotation_b: An updater MUST copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits of its input file, MUST NOT set any other: no writer under this text originates an ignore-lane bit...
findings.byte_level_rationale: An updater built strictly from edition B's text may emit a trailer with an ignore-lane bit cleared that the input file carried, since B states no prohibition against clearing it; an updater built from edition A's text is explicitly forbidden from doing so and must emit the bit unchanged. On the same input file and the same requested edit, the two implementations can commit different trailer 'flags' byte values.

findings.location_a: Section 20.3 step 2 (an appender's treatment of a carried-forward defective record, [R-LIF-01], cross-referencing Section 20.4)
findings.location_b: Section 20.3 step 2, same paragraph, same rule tag [R-LIF-01]
findings.title: Edition B turns a conditional 'MUST NOT drop the record' into an unconditional one, contradicting its own Section 20.4 drop licence
findings.detail: Edition A states that an appender carrying forward a structure it cannot repair 'MUST NOT drop the record save where Section 20.4 licenses the drop' - explicitly harmonized with Section 20.4's later rule that a record governed by MU=0,PE=0 flags MAY be dropped by an appender in any commit it is otherwise free to make. Edition B drops the exception clause, leaving an unconditional 'MUST NOT drop the record.' Section 20.4's MU=0,PE=0 drop licence is unchanged and present verbatim in both editions, so edition B alone now contains an internal contradiction between Section 20.3's absolute prohibition and Section 20.4's explicit permission for the same class of record.
findings.quotation_a: ...it MUST NOT repair the defect — [R-LIF-01] freezes the committed prefix — and MUST NOT drop the record save where §20.4 licenses the drop.
findings.quotation_b: ...it MUST NOT repair the defect — [R-LIF-01] freezes the committed prefix — and MUST NOT drop the record.
findings.byte_level_rationale: An updater built strictly from edition B's Section 20.3 text would refuse to drop a defective MU=0,PE=0 record it is carrying forward unmodified, stranding it in the new directory; an updater built from edition A's text (or from edition B's own Section 20.4, if it noticed the contradiction and resolved it toward the more specific rule) would drop it and reclaim the slot. The two implementations emit different directory bytes for the same input file and the same requested commit.

findings.location_a: Section 20.3 step 4, worked example ('Superseding one 100,000-byte stored tile of a 32-tile interleaved layer')
findings.title: Edition B's worked example restates 32·20+4 as 664 instead of the correct 644
findings.detail: 32 x 20 + 4 = 644, matching edition A's stated figure and matching the general index-region-size formula (entry_count x 20 + ceil(entry_count/2^16) x 4) that is unchanged and identical in both editions elsewhere (e.g. register row L2). Edition B states 664 for the same computation in its own worked example, an arithmetic error introduced during editing. The example is inside a non-normative 'Example' block, so no reader/writer conformance obligation is defined by the number itself, but an implementer calibrating their own implementation against the document's own worked figures (as both reader-implementer walks did for a different worked example in Section 7.4/15.4) could be misled into producing an incorrectly sized index region if they trusted edition B's stated total over deriving it from the formula.
findings.quotation_a: the layer's full new index region (32 · 20 + 4 = 644 bytes — one entry re-pointed, 31 byte-identical)
findings.quotation_b: the layer's full new index region (32 · 20 + 4 = 664 bytes — one entry re-pointed, 31 byte-identical)
findings.byte_level_rationale: The binding rule is the general formula, unchanged and correct in both editions outside this example, so a reader that implements the formula (rather than hard-coding the example's number) computes the same size under either edition; I do not mark this true because no register row or conformance rule is keyed to the example's specific figure, though the risk of a miscalibrated implementation trusting the wrong worked number is real and worth flagging.

findings.location_a: Section 20.4 (re-emission and preservation, introducing the MU/PE obligation table, [R-CNT-22]/[R-WRT-05] context)
findings.title: Edition B inverts which record types the MU=1 re-emission row reaches, contradicting its own next clause
findings.detail: Edition A states the table's MU=1 row 'reaches only a type the updater does not implement,' immediately followed by 'so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites' - a self-consistent pair of clauses. Edition B changes only the first clause to 'reaches every type, implemented or not,' while leaving the second clause ('so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites') untouched. The result in edition B is a single sentence that asserts the MU=1 row covers implemented types and then, in its own very next clause, concludes that implemented types are governed only by the PE bit - which is true only if the MU=1 row does not reach them. Edition A is internally consistent; edition B is self-contradictory at exactly this point.
findings.quotation_a: Its MU = 1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement — an updater implements both registered types and understands an unregistered type it implements from its definition, modifying their records as §20.3 and that definition provide — so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites:
findings.quotation_b: Its MU = 1 row reaches every type, implemented or not — an updater implements both registered types and understands an unregistered type it implements from its definition, modifying their records as §20.3 and that definition provide — so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites:
findings.byte_level_rationale: An implementer reading edition B's first clause literally could conclude that a record of an implemented type, when its governing flags happen to be MU=1, still falls under the MU=1 row's 'MUST NOT modify the scope the record governs' obligation, and refuse an edit that edition A's self-consistent text (and edition B's own second clause) would permit via Section 20.3's per-type rules; a different implementer reading only the second clause would follow edition A's behavior. Two conforming-per-edition-B implementations can diverge on the same file where two conforming-per-edition-A implementations converge.

findings.location_a: Section 20.4 (the sentence immediately after 'A commit MAY therefore drop a layer record, and the drop takes the layer whole')
findings.title: Edition B omits the exception that an unimplemented critical sub-record blocks a layer from being dropped at all
findings.detail: Edition A states that a layer carrying an unimplemented, critical (MU=1) sub-record cannot be dropped by a commit, because dropping the layer would itself be 'a modification of the scope [that sub-record] governs,' which the MU=1 row (present unchanged in both editions' table two rows above) forbids. Edition B omits this sentence entirely, leaving its preceding sentence ('A commit MAY therefore drop a layer record, and the drop takes the layer whole... whatever their PE bits') reading as an unqualified licence with no stated exception anywhere in edition B for this case.
findings.quotation_a: ...so a dropped layer's sub-records and their extents go with it whatever their PE bits. One sub-record blocks the drop, a sub-record of a type the updater does not implement with MU = 1, the drop being a modification of the scope it governs (the table's first row). A commit never removes a user-metadata record from a scope it keeps...
findings.quotation_b: ...so a dropped layer's sub-records and their extents go with it whatever their PE bits. A commit never removes a user-metadata record from a scope it keeps...
findings.byte_level_rationale: An updater built strictly from edition B's text may drop a layer that carries an unimplemented MU=1 sub-record, emitting a new directory without that layer or its sub-records; an updater built from edition A's text (and consistent with edition B's own MU=1 table row) refuses that drop entirely. On the same input file and the same requested edit, the two implementations commit different directory bytes.

findings.location_a: Section 21.2, register row F19, Instances cell
findings.location_b: Section 21.2, register row F19, Instances cell
findings.title: Register row F19's Instances cell narrows from 'bits 0-15' in edition A to 'bits 0-7' in edition B, matching only in A its own Condition text
findings.detail: Both editions' F19 Condition cell reads identically: 'Any bit of the flags incompat lane (bits 0-15) is set...'. Edition A's Instances cell reads 'flags bits 0-15,' matching the Condition exactly. Edition B's Instances cell reads 'flags bits 0-7,' narrower than its own Condition text and narrower than edition A's parallel cell. This confirms reader-B's own self-reported finding (readerb-02) as a genuine, edition-B-only defect rather than a pre-existing inconsistency shared by both editions - edition A has no analogous mismatch. The governing rule [R-CNT-08] is identical, unqualified, and covers all of bits 0-15 in both editions, so no conforming reader's accept/reject behavior changes; the loss is confined to the register's own internal consistency and its corpus-coverage promise (Section 21.1's 'at least one vector per instance'), which in edition B, read literally, no longer promises test-vector coverage of incompat-lane bits 8-15.
findings.quotation_a: | F19 | Any bit of the flags incompat lane (bits 0-15) is set; this text defines no flag bits, so every such bit is unimplemented | flags bits 0-15 | reader | open | `[R-CNT-08]` |
findings.quotation_b: | F19 | Any bit of the flags incompat lane (bits 0-15) is set; this text defines no flag bits, so every such bit is unimplemented | flags bits 0-7 | reader | open | `[R-CNT-08]` |
findings.byte_level_rationale: The governing rule [R-CNT-08] is unqualified and identical across bits 0-15 in both editions, and Section 21.1 (present in both) states that where a row's cited rule and its own cells diverge, the rule governs - so no conforming reader's accept or reject decision on any actual file changes between editions; the divergence is confined to the register's own stated conformance-vector coverage promise, not to reader behavior.

result.summary: A full `diff` of the two 4900+-line edition files (proof of exhaustiveness: the six hunks' line-count deltas sum to exactly -4, matching 4981-4977 precisely, so no seventh hunk was missed) shows the two texts are byte-identical everywhere except six points, all inside the writer/updater machinery (§6.3, §20.3, §20.4, §21.2) this charter is about. Three are real, previously-unflagged LOSS/CONTRADICTION defects unique to edition B: (1) the sentence stating that an unimplemented-type MU=1 sub-record blocks a licensed layer-drop is present in A and entirely absent from B, leaving B's "the drop takes the layer whole ... whatever their PE bits" unqualified where A is qualified — a real accept/reject divergence for a layer carrying such a sub-record; (2) A's general "MUST NOT drop the record" rule for anything an appender carries forward explicitly exempts §20.4's licensed drops ("save where §20.4 licenses the drop"); B states the same rule with no exemption, directly contradicting §20.4's own unchanged "an appender MAY drop the record" permission a few dozen lines later — B is internally self-contradictory where A is not; (3) B's own sentence "Its MU = 1 row reaches every type, implemented or not" directly contradicts the very next clause it shares with A verbatim, "so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites" — A's original "reaches only a type the updater does not implement" is the coherent premise that clause requires. A fourth defect, unique to B, sits in the §21.2 register: row F19's machine-readable field column says "flags bits 0-7" while its own prose cell and every other mention of the incompat lane in both editions says "bits 0-15" — an internal inconsistency that could cause a register-driven implementation of B to under-check the incompat lane. A fifth (already caught by walker B as writerb-01, and now confirmed as a genuine cross-edition difference rather than a self-contained observation) is the §20.3 worked-example arithmetic itself: A's Example correctly computes 644, B's states 664 — non-normative (Example-labelled, governed by the identical, correct `[R-CNT-17]` formula in both editions) so no byte-level effect on real output, but a real defect unique to B. A sixth difference (dropping "MUST NOT clear them" from the ignore-lane copy-forward rule) is EQUIVALENT — redundant with "copy forward" itself, no byte-level effect. Both walks' own findings (writera-01's zero-copy drop-and-recreate ambiguity, writera-02's cross-layer slab-recheck ambiguity) were checked against the other edition and found to rest on byte-identical text in both editions — shared indeterminacies, not divergences. All eight probes (W1-W8) were checked at their cited passages in both editions: W1, W3, W5, W6, W7, W8 rest on identical text in both editions (the walkers' answer differences, where any exist, are completeness/style only); W2 is the one probe where the answers genuinely diverge, tracing directly to the 644/664 defect above; W4's answers agree (both correctly built from the unchanged §20.4 table) but sit adjacent to the newly found step-2 contradiction unique to B.

findings.detail: A states, immediately after the persistence table, that a layer otherwise licensed for drop (its own record is registry-fixed PE=0) cannot actually be dropped if it carries a sub-record of an unimplemented type with MU=1, because the drop would modify the very scope that sub-record's MU=1 status protects. An implementer building strictly from B's stated text has nothing in this passage to stop them concluding a whole-layer drop is unconditional; an implementer of A cannot reach that conclusion. Walker A's own transcript explicitly quotes and relies on this sentence for its layer-drop analysis; walker B's transcript never mentions it, because it is not in B's edition.
findings.quotation_a: A commit MAY therefore drop a layer record, and the drop takes the layer whole: a sub-record's flags govern it within a layer the updater keeps, so a dropped layer's sub-records and their extents go with it whatever their PE bits. One sub-record blocks the drop, a sub-record of a type the updater does not implement with MU = 1, the drop being a modification of the scope it governs (the table's first row). A commit never removes a user-metadata record from a scope it keeps...

result.summary: The two editions are byte-identical except for six small, localized edits (a net 4-line length difference across ~4,980 lines), established by an exhaustive `diff`, not sampling. None of the six edits falls inside any passage either walker cited for probes V1-V6 or for its own findings — confirmed by reading every cited passage (section 2.3, 21.6, 10.2, 17.4/R-COD-11, 20.3-step-4/9.7, F25/L46, 21.1, the R-CNT-17 formula and its worked instances) in both editions and finding them byte-identical. Consequently every V1-V6 wording difference between the two walks is EQUIVALENT (same source text, different phrasing), and both walks' own OBSERVATION findings (verifiera-01/02, verifierb-01/02) rest on passages present, verbatim, in the other edition too, so none is unique to one edition. The substantive fidelity content of this round is the six diff hunks themselves, none of which either walker's probes touched: (1) section 20.4 inverts which records an updater's MU=1 preservation row governs ("only a type the updater does not implement" in A becomes "every type, implemented or not" in B), leaving B's own next clause ("so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites") no longer following from its stated premise — a genuine LOSS and an internal inconsistency unique to B; (2) the same local edit drops A's sentence naming exactly which sub-record blocks a layer drop, with no replacement in B; (3) section 20.3 step 2's appender drop-prohibition drops A's exception "save where section 20.4 licenses the drop," leaving B's absolute prohibition in unremarked tension with section 20.4's explicit MAY-drop license for PE=0 records; (4) a worked example's index-region arithmetic is wrong in B (32*20+4=664) against the correct value both editions' own unchanged R-CNT-17 formula yields (644), matching A's figure and a second unchanged worked instance of the same formula elsewhere; (5) the F19 register row's Instances cell says "bits 0-7" in B against "bits 0-15" in both the row's own unchanged Condition cell and the unchanged running prose, an internal contradiction unique to B with a narrow but real effect on mechanically-enumerated test-vector completeness; (6) a redundant clause ("MUST NOT clear them") is dropped from an ignore-lane preservation sentence without changing the obligation, which I score EQUIVALENT rather than LOSS since "copy forward" already entails not clearing. All six are outside the verifier's own certification obligations in the strict sense (updater/appender/writer-conduct and register-bookkeeping matters), which is why the verifier probes never surfaced them, but they are genuine divergences under the stated byte-level test for "an implementation built from the document," and four of the six are LOSS-classified defects unique to edition B.
