findings.title: B reverses the MU=1 row's stated reach from 'only unimplemented types' to 'every type, implemented or not,' while its own next clause still assumes the narrower reading

B: 'Its MU = 1 row reaches every type, implemented or not ... so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites.' Under A, since the updater implements T, the MU=1 row does not reach it, and the edit proceeds normally. Under B taken at its own stated premise, the MU=1 row's 'MUST NOT modify' obligation now reaches this implemented-type record too, barring the identical edit -- a different accept/reject verdict, and different output bytes (no modified extent ever written under B), for the same requested edit on the same input.

Its Instances cell -- the column the document's own reading guide (§1) says test vectors should be built against ('test vectors cite those identifiers rather than prose positions') -- reads 'flags bits 0-15' in A (matching the Condition cell and §6.3's unchanged prose) and 'flags bits 0-7' in B (covering only half the incompat lane, disagreeing with its own row's Condition cell). A verifier built from B's narrowed register alone (bits 0-7 only) never tests bit 10 under F19, finds nothing else in the row to catch it, and certifies the file conforming -- a real, differing verdict on one concrete, constructed file.

B omits this sentence. But the very same rule is already stated, unchanged, in the MU=1 row of §20.4's preservation table three paragraphs earlier in both editions: 'At layer scope an unknown critical record blocks modification of that layer, its drop included.' The removed sentence in A was purely a restatement for this specific paragraph's context; its absence in B does not remove the governing rule, which the table still states in full for both editions.
findings.quotation_a: One sub-record blocks the drop, a sub-record of a type the updater does not implement with MU = 1, the drop being a modification of the scope it governs (the table's first row).
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: The MU=1 preservation-table row, byte-identical in both editions, already states that an unknown critical (MU=1, unimplemented) record blocks modification of its layer 'its drop included' -- so a B-faithful updater is bound by the same rule regardless of this paragraph's restatement being removed; no output bytes or verdict differ.

findings.location_a: Section 6.3 (an updater's ignore-lane flag-bit obligations, governing rule [R-CNT-08])
findings.location_b: Section 6.3, same paragraph, same rule tag [R-CNT-08]
findings.title: Edition B drops the explicit 'MUST NOT clear them' obligation for an updater's unknown ignore-lane bits
findings.detail: Edition A imposes three distinct obligations on an updater regarding an ignore-lane bit (bits 16-31) it does not understand: it MUST copy the bit forward, it MUST NOT clear it, and it MUST NOT set any other such bit. Edition B states only the first and third obligations, dropping the middle clause entirely. 'Copy forward' alone does not unambiguously forbid an updater from zeroing a specific bit it considers meaningless while otherwise regenerating the trailer's flags word from the file's overall feature set; the explicit 'MUST NOT clear them' in A is what forecloses that reading. An implementer building strictly from B's text could conclude it is permitted to clear an unknown ignore-lane bit during a rewrite or append, since B states no prohibition against it, whereas an implementer building from A is explicitly barred from doing so.
findings.quotation_a: An updater MUST copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits of its input file, MUST NOT clear them, and MUST NOT set any other: no writer under this text originates an ignore-lane bit...
findings.quotation_b: An updater MUST copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits of its input file, MUST NOT set any other: no writer under this text originates an ignore-lane bit...
findings.byte_level_rationale: An updater built strictly from edition B's text may emit a trailer with an ignore-lane bit cleared that the input file carried, since B states no prohibition against clearing it; an updater built from edition A's text is explicitly forbidden from doing so and must emit the bit unchanged. On the same input file and the same requested edit, the two implementations can commit different trailer 'flags' byte values.

findings.location_a: Section 20.3 step 2 (an appender's treatment of a carried-forward defective record, [R-LIF-01], cross-referencing Section 20.4)
findings.location_b: Section 20.3 step 2, same paragraph, same rule tag [R-LIF-01]
findings.title: Edition B turns a conditional 'MUST NOT drop the record' into an unconditional one, contradicting its own Section 20.4 drop licence
findings.detail: Edition A states that an appender carrying forward a structure it cannot repair 'MUST NOT drop the record save where Section 20.4 licenses the drop' - explicitly harmonized with Section 20.4's later rule that a record governed by MU=0,PE=0 flags MAY be dropped by an appender in any commit it is otherwise free to make. Edition B drops the exception clause, leaving an unconditional 'MUST NOT drop the record.' Section 20.4's MU=0,PE=0 drop licence is unchanged and present verbatim in both editions, so edition B alone now contains an internal contradiction between Section 20.3's absolute prohibition and Section 20.4's explicit permission for the same class of record.
findings.quotation_a: ...it MUST NOT repair the defect — [R-LIF-01] freezes the committed prefix — and MUST NOT drop the record save where §20.4 licenses the drop.
findings.quotation_b: ...it MUST NOT repair the defect — [R-LIF-01] freezes the committed prefix — and MUST NOT drop the record.
findings.byte_level_rationale: An updater built strictly from edition B's Section 20.3 text would refuse to drop a defective MU=0,PE=0 record it is carrying forward unmodified, stranding it in the new directory; an updater built from edition A's text (or from edition B's own Section 20.4, if it noticed the contradiction and resolved it toward the more specific rule) would drop it and reclaim the slot. The two implementations emit different directory bytes for the same input file and the same requested commit.

findings.location_a: Section 20.3 step 4, worked example ('Superseding one 100,000-byte stored tile of a 32-tile interleaved layer')
findings.title: Edition B's worked example restates 32·20+4 as 664 instead of the correct 644
findings.detail: 32 x 20 + 4 = 644, matching edition A's stated figure and matching the general index-region-size formula (entry_count x 20 + ceil(entry_count/2^16) x 4) that is unchanged and identical in both editions elsewhere (e.g. register row L2). Edition B states 664 for the same computation in its own worked example, an arithmetic error introduced during editing. The example is inside a non-normative 'Example' block, so no reader/writer conformance obligation is defined by the number itself, but an implementer calibrating their own implementation against the document's own worked figures (as both reader-implementer walks did for a different worked example in Section 7.4/15.4) could be misled into producing an incorrectly sized index region if they trusted edition B's stated total over deriving it from the formula.
findings.quotation_a: the layer's full new index region (32 · 20 + 4 = 644 bytes — one entry re-pointed, 31 byte-identical)
findings.quotation_b: the layer's full new index region (32 · 20 + 4 = 664 bytes — one entry re-pointed, 31 byte-identical)
findings.byte_level_rationale: The binding rule is the general formula, unchanged and correct in both editions outside this example, so a reader that implements the formula (rather than hard-coding the example's number) computes the same size under either edition; I do not mark this true because no register row or conformance rule is keyed to the example's specific figure, though the risk of a miscalibrated implementation trusting the wrong worked number is real and worth flagging.

findings.location_a: Section 20.4 (re-emission and preservation, introducing the MU/PE obligation table, [R-CNT-22]/[R-WRT-05] context)
findings.title: Edition B inverts which record types the MU=1 re-emission row reaches, contradicting its own next clause
findings.detail: Edition A states the table's MU=1 row 'reaches only a type the updater does not implement,' immediately followed by 'so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites' - a self-consistent pair of clauses. Edition B changes only the first clause to 'reaches every type, implemented or not,' while leaving the second clause ('so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites') untouched. The result in edition B is a single sentence that asserts the MU=1 row covers implemented types and then, in its own very next clause, concludes that implemented types are governed only by the PE bit - which is true only if the MU=1 row does not reach them. Edition A is internally consistent; edition B is self-contradictory at exactly this point.
findings.quotation_a: Its MU = 1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement — an updater implements both registered types and understands an unregistered type it implements from its definition, modifying their records as §20.3 and that definition provide — so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites:
findings.quotation_b: Its MU = 1 row reaches every type, implemented or not — an updater implements both registered types and understands an unregistered type it implements from its definition, modifying their records as §20.3 and that definition provide — so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites:
findings.byte_level_rationale: An implementer reading edition B's first clause literally could conclude that a record of an implemented type, when its governing flags happen to be MU=1, still falls under the MU=1 row's 'MUST NOT modify the scope the record governs' obligation, and refuse an edit that edition A's self-consistent text (and edition B's own second clause) would permit via Section 20.3's per-type rules; a different implementer reading only the second clause would follow edition A's behavior. Two conforming-per-edition-B implementations can diverge on the same file where two conforming-per-edition-A implementations converge.

findings.location_a: Section 20.4 (the sentence immediately after 'A commit MAY therefore drop a layer record, and the drop takes the layer whole')
findings.title: Edition B omits the exception that an unimplemented critical sub-record blocks a layer from being dropped at all
findings.detail: Edition A states that a layer carrying an unimplemented, critical (MU=1) sub-record cannot be dropped by a commit, because dropping the layer would itself be 'a modification of the scope [that sub-record] governs,' which the MU=1 row (present unchanged in both editions' table two rows above) forbids. Edition B omits this sentence entirely, leaving its preceding sentence ('A commit MAY therefore drop a layer record, and the drop takes the layer whole... whatever their PE bits') reading as an unqualified licence with no stated exception anywhere in edition B for this case.
findings.quotation_a: ...so a dropped layer's sub-records and their extents go with it whatever their PE bits. One sub-record blocks the drop, a sub-record of a type the updater does not implement with MU = 1, the drop being a modification of the scope it governs (the table's first row). A commit never removes a user-metadata record from a scope it keeps...
findings.quotation_b: ...so a dropped layer's sub-records and their extents go with it whatever their PE bits. A commit never removes a user-metadata record from a scope it keeps...
findings.byte_level_rationale: An updater built strictly from edition B's text may drop a layer that carries an unimplemented MU=1 sub-record, emitting a new directory without that layer or its sub-records; an updater built from edition A's text (and consistent with edition B's own MU=1 table row) refuses that drop entirely. On the same input file and the same requested edit, the two implementations commit different directory bytes.

findings.location_a: Section 21.2, register row F19, Instances cell
findings.location_b: Section 21.2, register row F19, Instances cell

findings.location_a: §20.4, paragraph after the persistence table (line 3512-3514); qualifies §20.4's MU=1 row and the licensed layer-drop
findings.title: B omits entirely the rule that an unimplemented-type MU=1 sub-record blocks a licensed layer-drop
findings.detail: A states, immediately after the persistence table, that a layer otherwise licensed for drop (its own record is registry-fixed PE=0) cannot actually be dropped if it carries a sub-record of an unimplemented type with MU=1, because the drop would modify the very scope that sub-record's MU=1 status protects. B's corresponding text jumps straight from 'the drop takes the layer whole ... whatever their PE bits' to the next topic, with no such exception. An implementer building strictly from B's stated text has nothing in this passage to stop them concluding a whole-layer drop is unconditional; an implementer of A cannot reach that conclusion. Walker A's own transcript explicitly quotes and relies on this sentence for its layer-drop analysis; walker B's transcript never mentions it, because it is not in B's edition.
findings.quotation_a: A commit MAY therefore drop a layer record, and the drop takes the layer whole: a sub-record's flags govern it within a layer the updater keeps, so a dropped layer's sub-records and their extents go with it whatever their PE bits. One sub-record blocks the drop, a sub-record of a type the updater does not implement with MU = 1, the drop being a modification of the scope it governs (the table's first row). A commit never removes a user-metadata record from a scope it keeps...
findings.quotation_b: A commit MAY therefore drop a layer record, and the drop takes the layer whole: a sub-record's flags govern it within a layer the updater keeps, so a dropped layer's sub-records and their extents go with it whatever their PE bits. A commit never removes a user-metadata record from a scope it keeps...
findings.byte_level_rationale: For a layer whose own record is PE=0 (ordinarily droppable) but which carries one sub-record of an unimplemented type with MU=1: an implementation built from A alone must refuse to drop that layer via any commit; an implementation built from B alone, given nothing in this passage to forbid it, may emit a commit that drops the layer (and silently discards the MU=1 sub-record) — a different accept/reject and different output bytes for the identical operation on the identical input.

findings.title: B's general 'appender MUST NOT drop a carried-forward record' rule loses A's carve-out for §20.4's own licensed drops, contradicting §20.4 later in the same document
findings.detail: Both editions state, at §20.3 step 2, a general reliance rule: an appender must not repair a defect in anything it carries forward unmodified, and (A) must not drop the record 'save where §20.4 licenses the drop.' B drops the exception clause, leaving an unqualified 'MUST NOT drop the record.' A few dozen lines later, §20.4's table (identical, unchanged, in both editions) states 'an appender MAY drop the record in any commit it is otherwise free to make' for an MU=0/PE=0 record. A's step-2 sentence explicitly defers to that later permission; B's step-2 sentence, read on its own, flatly contradicts it. Neither walker's W4 answer surfaces this, since both built their W4 answer solely from the unchanged §20.4 table without needing or quoting the step-2 sentence.
findings.quotation_a: Against any other structure the appender carries forward, it MUST NOT repair the defect — [R-LIF-01] freezes the committed prefix — and MUST NOT drop the record save where §20.4 licenses the drop.
findings.quotation_b: Against any other structure the appender carries forward, it MUST NOT repair the defect — [R-LIF-01] freezes the committed prefix — and MUST NOT drop the record.
findings.byte_level_rationale: An implementation of B that resolves this self-contradiction by favoring the absolute step-2 statement (encountered first, in the procedure it is actually following) over the later, general §20.4 table would build an appender that never drops an MU=0/PE=0 record even when a caller asks for exactly the drop-only commit W4 describes — emitting a larger, different output file than any implementation of A, which has no such competing absolute statement to resolve.

findings.title: B's own sentence on the MU=1 row's scope contradicts the very next clause it shares verbatim with A
findings.detail: A states the MU=1 row of the persistence table 'reaches only a type the updater does not implement,' which is the premise the immediately following clause needs: 'so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites.' B changes the first clause to 'reaches every type, implemented or not' while leaving the second clause ('so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites') completely unchanged — the two clauses of the same sentence in B now assert incompatible things about whether the MU=1 row governs implemented types. A is internally coherent; B is not. This does not change either walker's W3/W8 answer (both probes stipulate an unimplemented type, the one case both readings agree on), but it leaves B with no coherent rule for a registered-but-untouched record whose stored/registry flags happen to carry MU=1.
findings.quotation_a: Its MU = 1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement — an updater implements both registered types and understands an unregistered type it implements from its definition, modifying their records as §20.3 and that definition provide — so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites
findings.quotation_b: Its MU = 1 row reaches every type, implemented or not — an updater implements both registered types and understands an unregistered type it implements from its definition, modifying their records as §20.3 and that definition provide — so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites
findings.byte_level_rationale: Outside the eight probes' exact scenarios: for an implemented type's record carrying MU=1 but not logically modified by a given commit, an implementation of A applies only the PE bit (no blocking); an implementation of B that takes 'reaches every type, implemented or not' literally could apply the MU=1 row's blocking/refuse-file behavior instead — a genuine accept/reject divergence on some file the probes do not happen to test.

findings.title: B's F19 register row is internally inconsistent: its machine-readable field column says bits 0-7, its own prose and every other mention of the incompat lane say bits 0-15
findings.detail: F19's descriptive text is identical in both editions: 'Any bit of the flags incompat lane (bits 0-15) is set.' The row's separate 'Field/bytes' column — the part a register-driven verifier or test-vector generator would read mechanically to know which bits to check — says 'flags bits 0-15' in A and 'flags bits 0-7' in B. Every other mention of the incompat lane in both files (§6.2's structural-field table, line 838; §6.3's prose, line 899; §9's summary at line ~4628) says bits 0-15 in both editions, with no corroborating 8-bit statement anywhere in B. This is an inconsistency unique to B between its own descriptive text and its own structured data for the same row.
findings.quotation_a: | F19 | Any bit of the flags incompat lane (bits 0-15) is set; this text defines no flag bits, so every such bit is unimplemented | flags bits 0-15 | reader | open | `[R-CNT-08]` |
findings.quotation_b: | F19 | Any bit of the flags incompat lane (bits 0-15) is set; this text defines no flag bits, so every such bit is unimplemented | flags bits 0-7 | reader | open | `[R-CNT-08]` |
findings.byte_level_rationale: An implementation of B that builds its open-time check mechanically from this row's field column checks only bits 0-7 for F19 and would accept a file with, e.g., bit 10 set (an unimplemented incompat bit) — a file an implementation built from A, or from B's own F19 prose, must reject-file. Not one of the eight writer probes directly, but inside the register a writer's own output (and any updater preserving an input) is measured against.

findings.title: Confirms writerb-01 as a genuine cross-edition divergence: A's worked example is arithmetically correct (644), B's is not (664)
findings.detail: Both editions' Example is otherwise word-for-word identical (confirmed by diff: this is the only differing token in the whole passage). A states '32 · 20 + 4 = 644 bytes,' which is correct and matches [R-CNT-17]'s formula (identical, correct, in both editions). B states '32 · 20 + 4 = 664 bytes,' which is not correct. Walker A quoted A's correct figure straight from the text; walker B independently recomputed and caught B's error as writerb-01, calling it non-normative since the block is Example-labelled under [R-CNF-01] (identical rule, both editions). I confirm here that A does not share this defect — A's own worked example is right — so per the charter's instruction to check a walk's own finding against the other edition, this is a defect unique to B, not a shared one.
findings.quotation_a: Superseding one 100,000-byte stored tile of a 32-tile interleaved layer appends: the new payload (100,000 bytes), the layer's full new index region (32 · 20 + 4 = 644 bytes — one entry re-pointed, 31 byte-identical)...
findings.quotation_b: Superseding one 100,000-byte stored tile of a 32-tile interleaved layer appends: the new payload (100,000 bytes), the layer's full new index region (32 · 20 + 4 = 664 bytes — one entry re-pointed, 31 byte-identical)...
findings.byte_level_rationale: The passage is labelled 'Example.' in both editions and [R-CNF-01] (identical text, both editions) makes it non-normative; real output size is governed by [R-CNT-17]'s formula, which is unchanged and correct in both editions. No conforming implementation's actual bytes or accept/reject verdict is controlled by this Example's stated total in either edition — only a reader hand-checking a test vector against the Example's own number would be misled, and only in B.

findings.title: B drops the redundant 'MUST NOT clear them' clause from the ignore-lane copy-forward rule; no behavioral change
findings.detail: A states three obligations for an updater's ignore-lane bits: copy forward, must not clear them, must not set any other. B states two: copy forward, must not set any other. 'Copy forward X' already means the output's bits equal the input's bits exactly, which is violated exactly as much by clearing a set bit as by setting an unset one; neither edition's register or §20.5 rewriter-specific restatement (identical in both) separately distinguishes 'cleared' from 'failed to copy forward' as different violations.
findings.quotation_a: An updater MUST copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits of its input file, MUST NOT clear them, and MUST NOT set any other: no writer under this text originates an ignore-lane bit...
findings.quotation_b: An updater MUST copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits of its input file, MUST NOT set any other: no writer under this text originates an ignore-lane bit...
findings.byte_level_rationale: An implementation satisfying B's 'copy forward ... MUST NOT set any other' necessarily also does not clear any bit, since copying forward a bit that was set means it remains set in the output; there is no implementation that could satisfy B's stated rule while violating A's dropped clause.

findings.title: writera-01's zero-copy drop-and-recreate ambiguity rests on text that is byte-identical in both editions — a shared indeterminacy, not a divergence
findings.detail: Walker A's finding (writera-01) that a same-commit drop-and-recreate might legitimately re-point new index entries at the very extents the same commit's drop just vacated — achieving a forbidden fill-change's effect at zero storage cost for padding-free tiles — is built on the sentence 'a commit MAY drop the layer (§20.4) and add a new one under its name and other declarations, the new layer being new whatever bytes its entries address, the dropped layer's former extents included.' This sentence, and the surrounding §9.1/[R-CNT-13] rules walker A cites as not resolving it, are confirmed byte-identical in edition B. The ambiguity is present equally in both editions; it is not something one edition states and the other does not.
findings.quotation_a: a commit MAY drop the layer (§20.4) and add a new one under its name and other declarations, the new layer being new whatever bytes its entries address, the dropped layer's former extents included, §5.2's partition being over the new state alone.
findings.quotation_b: a commit MAY drop the layer (§20.4) and add a new one under its name and other declarations, the new layer being new whatever bytes its entries address, the dropped layer's former extents included, §5.2's partition being over the new state alone.
findings.byte_level_rationale: The two editions are byte-identical at this passage and at every rule walker A cites as bearing on it (confirmed by full-file diff showing no hunk in this range), so no implementation would differ between an A-only and a B-only build on this point — whatever the ambiguity resolves to, it resolves the same way (or stays equally open) in both.

findings.title: writera-02's cross-layer slab-recheck ambiguity rests on text that is byte-identical in both editions — a shared indeterminacy, not a divergence
findings.detail: Walker A's finding (writera-02) — that no single passage states whether committing to layer X ever requires re-verifying an untouched, slab-declared layer Y's invariants — is built on [R-WRT-03]'s general reliance principle and §11.1's Rationale note on grid-count-unchanged growth. Every line walker A cites for [R-WRT-03] falls outside all six diff hunks, and I confirmed the corresponding B line numbers (each shifted by the small, cumulative offset the six earlier hunks introduce) hold identical text. The ambiguity is shared equally by both editions.

findings.quotation_b: Structures the commit neither modifies nor relies on impose no further obligation. `[R-WRT-03]`

findings.location_a: §20.4 Re-emission and preservation (updater MU=1 row scope)
findings.location_b: §20.4 Re-emission and preservation (updater MU=1 row scope)

One sub-record blocks the drop, a sub-record of a type the updater does not implement with MU = 1, the drop being a modification of the scope it governs (the table's first row). findings.location_b: §20.3 The append procedure, step 2 (drop prohibition, no carve-out)

findings.detail: Both editions state the index-region-size formula identically and unchanged elsewhere (entry_count×20 + ⌈entry_count/2¹⁶⌉×4; also confirmed via a second, unchanged worked instance yielding 84 for entry_count=4). findings.quotation_a: the layer's full new index region (32 · 20 + 4 = 644 bytes — one entry re-pointed, 31 byte-identical)
findings.quotation_b: the layer's full new index region (32 · 20 + 4 = 664 bytes — one entry re-pointed, 31 byte-identical)
findings.byte_level_rationale: 32*20+4 computed in build.py = 644, matching A and contradicting B's printed 664 for the identical formula and inputs; a fixture built to match B's stated byte count would not match one built from A's (or from the formula itself).

findings.location_a: §20.4, paragraph before the preservation table (lines 3497-3498), governs [R-WRT-05]'s table
findings.title: B reverses the MU=1 row's stated reach from 'only unimplemented types' to 'every type, implemented or not,' while its own next clause still assumes the narrower reading
findings.detail: A: 'Its MU = 1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement ... so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites.' B: 'Its MU = 1 row reaches every type, implemented or not ... so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites.' B's premise and conclusion are now mutually inconsistent: if MU=1 truly reached implemented types too, PE would not be the *only* thing that bites for them (MU=1's own 'retain byte-identical, MUST NOT modify the scope' obligation would also apply). A's version is internally consistent. Concretely: an updater implementing an unregistered type T from its own definition (per this same paragraph's own rule that such a type's governing flags come from its definition) wants to edit one of T's sub-records whose governing flags happen to be MU=1, PE=0. Under A, since the updater implements T, the MU=1 row does not reach it, and the edit proceeds normally. Under B taken at its own stated premise, the MU=1 row's 'MUST NOT modify' obligation now reaches this implemented-type record too, barring the identical edit -- a different accept/reject verdict, and different output bytes (no modified extent ever written under B), for the same requested edit on the same input.
findings.quotation_a: The table states what an updater owes a record it does not logically modify, read under whichever flags govern it. Its MU = 1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement — an updater implements both registered types and understands an unregistered type it implements from its definition, modifying their records as §20.3 and that definition provide — so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites:
findings.quotation_b: The table states what an updater owes a record it does not logically modify, read under whichever flags govern it. Its MU = 1 row reaches every type, implemented or not — an updater implements both registered types and understands an unregistered type it implements from its definition, modifying their records as §20.3 and that definition provide — so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites:
findings.byte_level_rationale: For an updater editing an implemented-but-MU=1-flagged sub-record of an unregistered type it defines itself: an A-faithful implementation writes new bytes for the modified extent; a B-faithful implementation (following B's stated premise literally) refuses the edit and emits no modified extent, or drops the whole layer instead -- different bytes, different verdict, same input and same requested edit.

findings.title: Register row F19's Instances cell narrows from 'flags bits 0-15' to 'flags bits 0-7,' disagreeing with its own unchanged Condition cell and with §6.3's unchanged prose
findings.detail: Row F19's Condition cell is byte-identical in both editions: 'Any bit of the flags incompat lane (bits 0-15) is set...'. Its Instances cell -- the column the document's own reading guide (§1) says test vectors should be built against ('test vectors cite those identifiers rather than prose positions') -- reads 'flags bits 0-15' in A (matching the Condition cell and §6.3's unchanged prose) and 'flags bits 0-7' in B (covering only half the incompat lane, disagreeing with its own row's Condition cell). I built a concrete 128-byte file (f19-bit10.tarn) that is a valid front block, an empty directory with correct CRC-32C, and a trailer with a verified-correct CRC-32C, whose flags field is 0x00000400 (bit 10 set) -- an incompat-lane bit outside 0-7 but inside 0-15, and every other §6.2 gate passes. Both editions' prose requires reject-file for this file (bit 10 is in the incompat lane, and this text defines no flag bits). A verifier built from A's register alone correctly rejects it. A verifier built from B's narrowed register alone (bits 0-7 only) never tests bit 10 under F19, finds nothing else in the row to catch it, and certifies the file conforming -- a real, differing verdict on one concrete, constructed file.
findings.quotation_a: | F19 | Any bit of the flags incompat lane (bits 0-15) is set; this text defines no flag bits, so every such bit is unimplemented | flags bits 0-15 | reader | open | `[R-CNT-08]` |
findings.quotation_b: | F19 | Any bit of the flags incompat lane (bits 0-15) is set; this text defines no flag bits, so every such bit is unimplemented | flags bits 0-7 | reader | open | `[R-CNT-08]` |
findings.byte_level_rationale: Constructed file f19-bit10.tarn (128 bytes, hex in transcript, flags=0x00000400, all other trailer/directory fields valid and CRC-correct): an implementation of A's register verdict = nonconforming/reject-file (bit 10 tested and caught); an implementation of B's narrowed register verdict = conforming (bit 10 never tested under F19). Same file, different certified verdict.

findings.title: B drops the standalone 'MUST NOT clear them' clause for updaters' ignore-lane bits, but the obligation survives unchanged elsewhere
findings.detail: A states three obligations for an updater regarding unknown ignore-lane bits: copy forward, MUST NOT clear them, MUST NOT set any other. B states only two: copy forward, MUST NOT set any other. However §6.2's trailer flags-field table row is byte-identical in both editions and already says such bits are 'carried forward unchanged by every updater (appender and rewriter alike)' -- which already forbids clearing. No implementation built from B alone would differ in behavior or output bytes from one built from A, since the same requirement is fully and independently stated in the unchanged table.
findings.quotation_a: An updater MUST copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits of its input file, MUST NOT clear them, and MUST NOT set any other: no writer under this text originates an ignore-lane bit...
findings.quotation_b: An updater MUST copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits of its input file, MUST NOT set any other: no writer under this text originates an ignore-lane bit...
findings.byte_level_rationale: Section 6.2's unchanged flags-field table cell ('carried forward unchanged by every updater') already forbids clearing any ignore-lane bit in both editions, so no updater built from B alone could conform while clearing such a bit -- the requirement is redundant, not lost, and no output bytes or verdict differ between editions.

findings.title: B drops the 'one sub-record blocks the drop' restatement, but the MU=1 table row already states the same rule
findings.detail: A's layer-drop paragraph adds an explicit restatement: an MU=1, unimplemented-type sub-record blocks a commit from dropping the whole layer, since the drop would modify the scope that sub-record governs. B omits this sentence. But the very same rule is already stated, unchanged, in the MU=1 row of §20.4's preservation table three paragraphs earlier in both editions: 'At layer scope an unknown critical record blocks modification of that layer, its drop included.' The removed sentence in A was purely a restatement for this specific paragraph's context; its absence in B does not remove the governing rule, which the table still states in full for both editions.
findings.quotation_a: One sub-record blocks the drop, a sub-record of a type the updater does not implement with MU = 1, the drop being a modification of the scope it governs (the table's first row).
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: The MU=1 preservation-table row, byte-identical in both editions, already states that an unknown critical (MU=1, unimplemented) record blocks modification of its layer 'its drop included' -- so a B-faithful updater is bound by the same rule regardless of this paragraph's restatement being removed; no output bytes or verdict differ.

findings.title: No outcome class defined for a reader lacking a mandatory (core) codec or filter
findings.detail: Every assigned codec (1-4) and filter (1-2) value is core: a conforming reader MUST implement all of them (R-CNF-03, restated at R-COD-03/R-COD-09). For the adjacent, well-specified cases the document is explicit: an invalid/reserved/experimental codec or filter value is reject-layer (L43/L45); a verifier unable to execute a codec reports 'cannot establish' (R-COD-11); and exactly two capability refusals are named as conforming-file-but-refused cases in §21.6's closing paragraph (an unimplemented format major, and an unimplemented top-level MU=1 record type). For a reader (not a verifier) lacking an assigned, core codec/filter it can't execute, R-COD-11's only statement is that such software 'is not a conforming reader' -- it disqualifies the implementation from the conformance class rather than prescribing any behavior, and is not reached by R-ERR-04's resource-decline licence (which governs §21.9's guarantee table) or by either of the two named capability refusals. An implementer building software that knowingly supports fewer than all four codecs has no textual answer for what a spec-following degraded behavior looks like here -- the document simply defines the question out of existence for conforming software. An implementer reading a different edition whose §17.4/§21.9 wording differs slightly (e.g. extending R-ERR-04's licence to cover this ground, or extending R-COD-11's 'cannot establish' framing to readers) would answer probe R3 differently.
findings.quotation_a: software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: A conforming reader is required, unconditionally, to implement all four codecs and both filters (R-CNF-03), so this scenario is definitionally impossible for any implementation the specification's acceptance/rejection obligations apply to. Resolving the gap would only add guidance for software that has already left the conformance class by the document's own terms; it changes no accept/reject/emit boundary for a conforming file or a conforming reader.

findings.title: No outcome class exists for a reader's own incapacity to execute an assigned/core enumerator (e.g. codec 3/zstd)
findings.detail: The document requires a conforming reader to implement every core codec, filter, layout, sample type, metadata encoding, and registered record type (R-CNF-03), and states that software failing one of these 'is not a conforming reader' - an actor-status disqualification, not an entry in section 21's outcome vocabulary (reject-file/-layer/-tile/ignore-record). Section 17.4 (R-COD-11) defines the reader-side outcome (reject-layer) only for a codec/filter value the file itself gets wrong (reserved or experimental), and defines a verifier's 'cannot establish' stance only for a verifier that cannot execute an otherwise-valid codec. Neither covers an ordinary reader meeting an assigned, core value it simply has not implemented (the probe's own scenario: codec 3/zstd declared, reader lacks zstd). Two implementations, both accepting every conforming file within the guaranteed limits and rejecting every register-condemned file, can diverge on such a file: one serves every reference-array byte for the zstd-coded layer, another refuses the whole file, another refuses only that layer, and another attempts a partial decode - the document licenses and forbids none of these explicitly, because by R-CNF-03's own terms the implementation lacking zstd is not 'a conforming reader' the moment it lacks it, so no requirement written for conforming readers binds it at all.
findings.quotation_a: software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: It changes whether a conforming file's layer's decoded sample bytes are ever returned at all (served vs. refused) and, if an implementer chooses to fail gracefully, at what scope (file vs. layer) that refusal would land - exactly an accept/reject divergence over the same conforming bytes.

findings.title: Register row F19's Instances cell (bits 0-7) is narrower than its own Condition text (bits 0-15)
findings.detail: Row F19's Condition column states the violation ranges over 'the flags incompat lane (bits 0-15)', but the same row's Instances cell reads only 'flags bits 0-7'. Section 21.1 states the Instances column enumerates what a conformance corpus builds for that row, with at least one vector per instance; on its face this cell under-enumerates bits 8-15, a gap the row's own text does not flag as a gap. This does not change reader behavior, because section 21.1 also states that where a row and the rule it cites diverge, the rule governs, and the governing rule (R-CNT-08) is unqualified across all of bits 0-15 - so it is a defect in the register's own internal consistency and in its stated corpus-coverage promise, not a behavior-affecting ambiguity.
findings.quotation_a: Any bit of the flags incompat lane (bits 0-15) is set... | flags bits 0-7 | reader | open | `[R-CNT-08]`
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: The governing rule R-CNT-08 is unqualified and controls over the Instances cell per section 21.1's own precedence clause, so no conforming reader's accept/reject decision over any byte changes; a corpus built strictly to this cell's letter could nonetheless ship without a vector for, e.g., bit 12, which is a coverage gap rather than a behavioral one.

findings.location_a: §9.1 (`[R-LIF-01]`); §20.3 step 4 ('a commit MAY drop the layer... and add a new one under its name and other declarations, the new layer being new whatever bytes its entries address, the dropped layer's former extents included'); `[R-CNT-13]`; `[R-WRT-04]`
findings.title: Same-commit drop-and-recreate may let a forbidden in-place fill change through byte-identically for padding-free tiles
findings.detail: The fixed-declaration bar (§20.3 step 4) forbids changing a stored layer's fill while it stores a tile, but explicitly permits dropping that layer and adding a new one under the same name in the same commit, whose entries may address 'the dropped layer's former extents.' Nothing I found forbids those new entries from pointing, unmodified, at the exact byte ranges the same commit's drop just vacated -- §9.1 only bars modifying bytes below the commit's starting F, not re-referencing them, and `[R-CNT-13]`'s single-ownership check runs against the resulting live state, where the old claim is already gone. If this reuse is legitimate, a commit can achieve the forbidden 'change fill on a stored tile' outcome at zero extra storage cost and with no detectable trace, for any tile with no padding position (where T4/T5 can't fire). An implementer following edition A alone would build a writer that either (a) allows this zero-copy drop-and-recreate reuse, producing a minimal-size commit, or (b) conservatively re-writes the tile payload as fresh bytes at a new placement -- two different minimum byte layouts for the identical logical operation, and I could not find text in edition A resolving which is required.
findings.quotation_a: a commit MAY drop the layer (§20.4) and add a new one under its name and other declarations, the new layer being new whatever bytes its entries address, the dropped layer's former extents included, §5.2's partition being over the new state alone.
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Resolving this changes which bytes a conforming implementation may emit: whether a drop-and-recreate commit's new tile-index entries may point, unwritten, at bytes the same commit's drop just vacated (a zero-copy commit) or must instead write fresh payload bytes at a new post-F placement (a commit whose minimum size includes at least one full tile payload plus a fresh index region) is a directly observable difference in emitted bytes for the identical logical edit.

findings.location_a: `[R-WRT-03]`; §11.1's Rationale note (grid-count-unchanged growth 'touches the directory alone')
findings.title: No single passage states whether an untouched, slab-declared layer's invariants are ever re-checked as a side effect of another layer's commit
findings.detail: `[R-WRT-03]` states the general updater reliance principle ('structures the commit neither modifies nor relies on impose no further obligation'), which implies a slab-declared layer Y untouched by a commit to layer X owes no re-check. Separately, §11.1's note describes a grid-count-unchanged growth as touching 'the directory alone,' which (combined with `[R-WRT-05]`'s byte-identical re-emission of untouched records) supports the same conclusion for layer Y specifically. I resolved this myself (no re-check owed, since Y's record and placement are unchanged either way), but I did not find one passage stating the cross-layer case -- 'committing to layer X never requires re-verifying layer Y's `[R-SLB-03]`/`[R-SLB-04]` invariants' -- directly, only two general principles I had to combine.
findings.quotation_a: Structures the commit neither modifies nor relies on impose no further obligation.
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: On my own reading this resolves to 'no additional check owed' and so does not change which bytes an implementation may emit or accept; I report it only because the specific cross-layer case is never stated in one place, only inferred by combining two general rules, and the charter asks for exactly this class of underdetermination even where I believe it resolves cleanly.

findings.location_a: §20.3, worked Example immediately following [R-WRT-04] ("Superseding one 100,000-byte stored tile of a 32-tile interleaved layer appends...")
findings.title: Worked append-example miscomputes the new index-region size: states 664 bytes where the arithmetic (and the document's own formula) gives 644
findings.detail: The document states the new tile-index region for a 32-entry layer is "32 · 20 + 4 = 664 bytes". Direct computation and the document's own normative formula in [R-CNT-17] (entry_count × 20 + ceil(entry_count/2^16) × 4) both give 32×20+4 = 644, not 664 — a 20-byte discrepancy in the example's stated arithmetic. Because this passage is labelled "Example.", [R-CNF-01] makes it non-normative, so no conforming implementation's actual output or acceptance decision is controlled by this number; the formula in [R-CNT-17] governs real bytes and is itself correct. The defect is confined to the illustration.
findings.quotation_a: "the layer's full new index region (32 · 20 + 4 = 664 bytes — one entry re-pointed, 31 byte-identical)"
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: The erroneous figure sits inside a block quote labelled 'Example.', which [R-CNF-01] makes non-normative; the normative sizing rule is [R-CNT-17]'s formula, which is correct and is what any conforming writer's index-region length and any conforming reader's/verifier's extent_length cross-check ([R-CNT-17]) actually apply. Fixing the example's arithmetic would not change one byte a conforming implementation may emit or must accept or reject.

findings.location_a: §2.3 (R-CNF-11), the cannot-establish trigger list; and §21.6's closing paragraph on the same structural pattern
findings.title: A file can be byte-predicate-conforming yet no verifier may ever certify it 'conforming'
findings.detail: R-CNF-11 unconditionally lists 'a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement (§21.6)' as a cannot-establish ground. §21.6, discussing the identical pattern (an experimental-range top-level record type carrying MU=1), states the file 'carries no violation at all' — i.e. it is a conforming file under the specification's own byte predicate. Since experimental values are by definition private and collision-unprotected (§10.3), no general verifier implements them all, so for this entire class of genuinely conforming files, an implementer following R-CNF-11 to the letter must never emit the verdict 'conforming' — only 'cannot establish' (or 'nonconforming' if something else is also wrong). An implementer who instead reasons from §21.6 alone ('no violation at all' -> report conforming) would violate R-CNF-11's explicit bar on certifying a file it cannot fully check.
findings.quotation_a: "when a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement (§21.6)" ... "the file in the second carries no violation at all."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: It fixes, for an entire structural family of inputs (top-level experimental-range MU=1 records), that a conforming verifier implementation may never emit the byte-level verdict 'conforming' no matter how completely it checks everything else in the file — a concrete, permanent constraint on what output such an implementation may ever produce for that input class.

findings.location_a: §21.1, the 'strict specializations' paragraph listing F1/F6, F1/F8, F35/F36, L24/L25, F21/F22, L10/L11 as an admittedly non-exhaustive example list
findings.title: Row-subsumption pairs beyond the six named examples are left to a re-derivable test, not an enumerated list
findings.detail: §21.1 gives a general, fully decidable test for when one register row is a strict specialization of another ('the property decides any pair') but explicitly declines to enumerate every pair that satisfies it beyond six named examples. A verifier or vector author encountering some other pair of rows with this relationship (if one exists elsewhere in the register) has no closed list to consult and must re-derive the property, which is an operational hazard for building a complete, correctly-attributed conformance corpus (R-VEC-02/R-VEC-03) even though it changes no accepted or rejected byte.
findings.quotation_a: "the property decides any pair and this list is not offered as closed."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: The outcome (scope and reject class) for a file exhibiting either row of a genuine subsumption pair is identical by construction ('necessarily exhibits another's'), so no byte a conforming implementation may emit, accept, or reject changes with which of the two row identifiers is cited — only the report/vector bookkeeping is affected.

findings.title: Codec/filter execution failure (R-COD-11) is not listed among the coverage-walk's own partial-total triggers
findings.detail: §5.2/§9.7 (R-LIF-08, R-CNT-21) enumerate exactly three things that make a verifier's coverage-walk slack total partial: a scope-level rejection blocking enumeration, a layer declined on resource grounds (R-ERR-04), or the verifier stopping at the first violation (R-CNF-11). R-COD-11's 'cannot execute a layer's codec or filter' capability decline is never named in that list. Since a layer's coverage-walk claimants (its extent slot, index-region checksums, and each entry's crc over stored bytes) are all establishable without invoking the codec or filter -- only §14's decoded-content obligations (R-SER-05, R-SER-08) require decoding -- an implementer following only §5.2/§9.7's literal trigger list could reasonably conclude (correctly, I believe, but only by inference) that a verifier stuck on R-COD-11 for one layer still reports an EXACT slack/live-state total for the whole file, even though it cannot certify. An implementer who instead assumed decode-inability must degrade the walk to 'partial' (by analogy with R-ERR-04) would produce a materially different verifier report from one who read the sections as I did.
findings.quotation_a: n/a
findings.quotation_b: Where the walk does not complete — a scope-level rejection blocks enumeration, the verifier declines a layer on resource grounds and so never enumerates its claimants ([R-ERR-04]), or it stops at the first violation ([R-CNF-11]) — the sum is reported as partial
findings.byte_level_rationale: This affects only the verifier's diagnostic report (whether the slack figure is labeled exact or partial) alongside a verdict that is already independently fixed at 'cannot establish' (or 'nonconforming', if the codec value is itself reserved/experimental) by R-COD-11/L43/L45. It does not change which file bytes a conforming writer may emit, nor which files a conforming reader must accept or reject -- only a secondary field of the verifier's own report.

findings.title: A commit that silently violates the fixed-declaration bar is undetectable by the verifier's certification model except by accident
findings.detail: §20.3 step 4 explicitly states that a commit changing a fixed declaration of a layer that stored a tile 'binds the commit as an actor' and carries 'no register row', and §9.7's own Note confirms the verifier's certification model has no access to prior generations at all ('does not depend on reconstructing the file's history'). The document is internally consistent and not contradictory here, but the practical consequence -- that a verifier can and, per the design, sometimes MUST certify a file whose last commit reinterpreted a stored tile's fill, type, codec, or geometry in place, provided the old bytes happen to still parse under the new declaration -- is easy for an implementer to miss, since every other structural change in §20.3-§20.5 has a corresponding register row or explicit non-violation entry, and this is the one place the document says outright that detection is sometimes simply unavailable to any actor.
findings.quotation_a: n/a
findings.quotation_b: This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself, the register enumerating file-conformance violations (§21.1) and the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit (§21.7, [R-ERR-01], [R-CNF-02])
findings.byte_level_rationale: This determines a real accept/reject outcome: given the SAME live-state bytes (a layer whose current declarations happen to still validate structurally against its stored tiles), a conforming verifier MUST certify the file even if that layer's declarations were in fact changed illegitimately across the last commit -- the certification result depends only on whether the current bytes pass every register row, never on the commit history that produced them.

findings.title: Slate A quiza-06: the editions' takers answer differently
findings.detail:
QUESTION: A layer stored at least one tile in generation N. Generation N+1's single commit both unstores every one of the layer's tiles (so the layer addresses tiles but stores none, i.e. becomes empty) and changes the layer's declared fill value for one channel. Is this a valid appender commit, or does it require declaring a new layer or performing a whole-file rewrite?
FROM A: requires declaring a new layer [medium] cites §20.3 step 4 (R-WRT-04); §20.4 (drop licence, R-CNT-22 fixed flags MU=0 PE=0 for layer records)
FROM B: requires declaring a new layer or performing a whole-file rewrite (not a valid appender commit) [high] cites §20.3 step 4 (`[R-WRT-04]`)
A's reasoning: Fill value is not among the permitted in-place changes to a layer that stored a tile in the superseded generation, and the empties-in-the-same-commit escape is explicitly closed. But the text also explicitly licenses dropping the layer (PE=0 registry-fixed) and adding a new one under the same name within a single appender commit, which is a 'new layer' operation rather than a whole-file rewrite. Since the question asks for a single verdict between the two named alternatives, and drop-and-recreate is achievable by an ordinary appender commit, 'new layer' is the more specific and achievable answer; a whole-file rewrite is not required to accomplish this particular outcome. Medium confidence because the question's phrasing could also be read as expecting 'rewrite' if the grader intends 'new layer' to mean a distinct name coexisting with the old one rather than drop+recreate under the same name.
B's reasoning: Fill value is one of the declarations fixed 'for as long as the layer stores a tile,' and the tense is the prior (superseded) generation's, so emptying the layer in the same commit does not free up the fill value for change.
findings.quotation_a: a commit does not earn an empty layer's freedom by emptying the layer as it re-declares it: a layer that stored a tile keeps its declarations through the commit that empties it... a commit MAY drop the layer (§20.4) and add a new one under its name and other declarations
findings.quotation_b: a layer that stored a tile keeps its declarations through the commit that empties it... [fill is] fixed for as long as the layer stores a tile... A commit MUST NOT change one of these; the change is a new layer, or a rewrite that re-declares it under a fresh file_id.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Mechanically detected divergence; the passes decide whether it is a loss, an addition, or a taker error, and whether it forks bytes.

findings.title: Slate A quiza-09: the editions' takers answer differently
findings.detail:
QUESTION: A layer is planar with channel count C = 3, and its declared geometry gives a spatial-tile count N = 70,000. What is the layer's entry_count, and what is the exact byte length of its tile-index region (entry array plus segment CRC array)?
FROM A: 210000, 4200016 [high] cites §11.2 (R-GEO-03, addressed-tile count C·N for planar); §7.4/§15.1 (R-CNT-17, index region formula)
FROM B: 210,000; 4,200,016 [high] cites §11.2 (addressed-tile count = C·N for planar); §7.4 (entry_count field); `[R-CNT-17]`
A's reasoning: entry_count = C*N = 3*70000 = 210000. Region length = 210000*20 + ceil(210000/65536)*4 = 4,200,000 + 4*4 = 4,200,016.
B's reasoning: entry_count = C*N = 3*70,000 = 210,000. Region length = 210,000*20 + ceil(210,000/65,536)*4 = 4,200,000 + 4*4 = 4,200,016.
findings.quotation_a: Under index_encoding 1, extent_length MUST equal entry_count × 20 + ⌈entry_count / 2¹⁶⌉ × 4
findings.quotation_b: extent_length MUST equal entry_count × 20 + ⌈entry_count / 2¹⁶⌉ × 4
findings.byte_level_rationale: Mechanically detected divergence; the passes decide whether it is a loss, an addition, or a taker error, and whether it forks bytes.

findings.title: Slate A quiza-13: the editions' takers answer differently
findings.detail:
QUESTION: A rewriter is regenerating a layer's tile-index region (because some of the layer's stored extents relocated) and, while classifying entries, meets one that §15.3 classifies reject-tile on a structural ground (for example: offset = sentinel, length != sentinel). Name the rewriter's two possible dispositions for this situation, and state which one is the only way this rewrite can still reclaim that layer's slack.
FROM A: drop the layer; refuse — dropping the layer reclaims slack [high] cites §20.5 (R-WRT-06, R-WRT-07); §20.4 (drop licence)
FROM B: drop the layer; refuse — dropping the layer is the only one that reclaims the layer's slack [high] cites §20.5 (regenerating a region; `[R-WRT-06]`; `[R-IDX-03]`)
A's reasoning: Only dropping the layer (omitting it from the rewrite's output) actually reclaims its slack; refusing means no new file is produced at all, so nothing is reclaimed.
B's reasoning: The two named dispositions are dropping the layer or refusing to rewrite; refusing means no rewrite output is produced at all (nothing reclaimed), whereas dropping the layer lets the rewrite proceed and reclaim the layer's slack, consistent with §20.5's discussion of a rewrite that drops a layer reclaiming what a commit would strand.

findings.title: Slate B quizb-01: the editions' takers answer differently
findings.detail:
QUESTION: A layer is declared planar, rank 3, with a single channel of sample type float64 (element size 8 bytes). Its three dimensions each have extent equal to their own tile extent: 1024, 1024, and 256 (so the layer addresses exactly one tile). The layer declares codec 4 (lz4). Compute this channel's decoded tile size in bytes, and state whether declaring codec 4 on this layer is conforming or a validity error. If it is a validity error, name the outcome class and the owning scope it falls at.
FROM A: Decoded tile size = 2,147,483,648 bytes (2^31 = P·B = 1024×1024×256 × 8). Declaring codec 4 (lz4) on this layer is a validity error: outcome class reject-layer (register row L44, governed by [R-COD-07]), owning scope layer. [high] cites §14.2 [R-SER-02] (decoded size = P·Bᶜ for a planar numeric channel); §11.2 (P = ∏Tᵢ); §17.2 [R-COD-07] (lz4 decoded-size cap 0x7E000000); §21.3 register row L44
FROM B: Decoded tile size = 2,147,483,648 bytes; declaring codec 4 (lz4) here is a validity error — outcome class reject-layer, owning scope layer. [high] cites §14.2 (decoded-size table, planar/numeric row); §17.2 [R-COD-07]; §21.3 register row L44
A's reasoning: P = 1024*1024*256 = 268,435,456; decoded size = P*8 (float64 element size) = 2,147,483,648 = 0x80000000, which exceeds the stated cap 0x7E000000 (2,113,929,216). [R-COD-07] makes this a validity error at layer scope, and register row L44 names the outcome reject-layer explicitly under the §21.3 table header 'Outcome: reject-layer'.
B's reasoning: P = 1024*1024*256 = 268,435,456; decoded size = P*8 (float64 element size) = 2,147,483,648, per §14.2's planar-numeric row (decoded size = P·Bᶜ). The lz4 cap in [R-COD-07] is 0x7E000000 = 2,113,929,216 bytes, quantified over the layer's addressed tiles (here, the one tile equals the full layer). 2,147,483,648 exceeds the cap, so codec 4 is a validity error, register row L44, outcome reject-layer, scope layer.

findings.quotation_b: Writers MUST NOT declare this codec for a layer any of whose addressed tiles' decoded size exceeds 0x7E000000 bytes ... a reader MUST treat such a declaration as a validity error at layer scope

findings.title: Slate B quizb-02: the editions' takers answer differently
findings.detail:
QUESTION: A remote reader opens a 10,000-byte TARN file by issuing a single speculative suffix-range request for the final 300 bytes of the file (byte offsets [9700, 10000)), and uses containment to decide whether a second request is needed. Does this reader's open leave the front signature block (bytes [0, 16)) resident? Per the document's rule, is this reader required to verify the front signature block by byte equality before other processing, or may it defer or omit that check?
FROM A: (a) not resident; (b) MAY defer or omit the front-signature-block verification. [high] cites §6.1 [R-CNT-04]; §19.1 step 1 (open algorithm)
FROM B: (a) not resident; (b) MAY defer or omit. [high] cites §6.1 [R-CNT-04]
A's reasoning: The reader's single speculative fetch is the suffix range [9700,10000), which does not include offset 0, so bytes [0,16) are not resident by [R-CNT-04]'s definition ('a speculative suffix window that reached offset 0' is the qualifying case, and this one did not reach it). Since residency is absent, the rule's second clause governs: the check may be deferred or omitted.
B's reasoning: The reader's single speculative request covers only bytes [9700,10000) of a 10,000-byte file, which does not include [0,16). Per [R-CNT-04], residency (not transport) governs the obligation; since obtaining the front block would need a further request, the reader MAY defer or omit verifying it.
findings.quotation_a: A reader that would have to issue a further range request to obtain those bytes MAY defer or omit the check

findings.title: Slate B quizb-05: the editions' takers answer differently
findings.detail:
QUESTION: A layer has two dimensions with extents (7, 7) and tile extents (5, 5), and one channel of type uint16 with declared fill value 0xBEEF. Consider the tile at tile coordinates (1, 1) (the high-edge tile along both axes). How many of that tile's sample positions are padding positions (i.e., lie outside the layer's extents)? For any one such padding position, what are the exact two stored bytes, in order, that a conforming stored tile must encode there for this channel (give them as upper-case hex byte pairs)?
FROM A: 21 padding positions. For any one such position, the two stored bytes in order are EF BE (little-endian encoding of the uint16 fill value 0xBEEF). [high] cites §11.2/§11.3 (grid arithmetic and padding); §14.5 [R-SER-05] (padding content = channel fill); §4.1 [R-ENC-01] (little-endian)
FROM B: 21 padding positions; EF BE. [high] cites §11.2 [R-GEO-03] (grid count); §11.3 [R-GEO-04] (padding positions); §14.5 [R-SER-05] (padding content); §4.1 [R-ENC-01] (little-endian)
A's reasoning: G=ceil(7/5)=2 per axis; tile (1,1) covers in-tile positions u in [0,5) mapping to coordinate 5+u, real only when 5+u<7 i.e. u in {0,1} (2 of 5 per axis). Real positions = 2*2=4 of 25 total, so padding = 21. §14.5 fixes padding content to the channel's recorded fill, and §4.1 makes all multi-byte fields little-endian, so 0xBEEF stores as bytes EF BE — mirroring §14.5's own worked example which stores fill 0xABCD as CD AB.
B's reasoning: G=ceil(7/5)=2 per axis; tile (1,1) has 2 real positions per axis (coords 5,6) out of 5, so 4 real of 25 total, 21 padding. Fill 0xBEEF stored little-endian is low byte then high byte: EF then BE.
findings.quotation_a: at every padding position, a writer MUST encode, for each channel the position carries, that channel's fill value
findings.quotation_b: at every padding position, a writer MUST encode, for each channel the position carries, that channel's fill value

findings.title: Slate B quizb-06: the editions' takers answer differently
findings.detail:
QUESTION: A planar layer has three channels declared in this order: 'r' (uint8, fill 10), 'g' (uint8, fill 20), 'b' (uint8, fill 30). What are the three channel values of the sample at that coordinate, in declared channel order (r, g, b)?

FROM B: (200, 20, 5) [high] cites §3.2 [R-MDL-01]; §13.3 [R-TYP-08]
A's reasoning: Planar layers make each channel's storedness independent (§3.2, §13.3). r and b are stored and decode bit-exactly per [R-MDL-02]/[R-TYP-04]; g's tile is the sentinel, so g reads as its recorded fill (20) per [R-TYP-06]/[R-TYP-08]. This exactly mirrors §13.3's own worked example of a planar layer with one channel sentinel among stored ones.

QUESTION: A layer is planar with a bool channel whose tile is a packed boolean plane (i.e., its decoded image is bit-packed per §14.3, not a byte-per-value plane). If filter 2 (byte-shuffle) is declared for this layer, what is the byte-shuffle stride s applied to this channel's packed plane, and what is the practical effect of applying filter 2 at that stride on the plane's stored bytes?

B's reasoning: §17.3 states this case verbatim and directly: a packed boolean plane's shuffle stride is 1, at which the byte-shuffle transform is the identity (no bytes moved).

findings.title: Slate B quizb-08: the editions' takers answer differently
findings.detail:
QUESTION: A verifier is checking a file. During its coverage walk, it reaches a layer whose stored-tile decode it declines purely on resource grounds (invoking the document's resource-limit provision), and, apart from that decline, it establishes no violation anywhere else in the file. What single verdict word does the verifier report for the file as a whole — one of: conforming, nonconforming, cannot establish? And when it reports the file's slack-byte total, must that total be reported as complete or as partial?
FROM A: Verdict: cannot establish. Slack total: partial. [high] cites §2.3 [R-CNF-11]; §5.2 [R-CNT-21]; §9.7 [R-LIF-08]
FROM B: cannot establish; complete. [high] cites §2.3 [R-CNF-11]; §5.2 [R-CNT-21]
A's reasoning: [R-CNF-11] lists declining a layer's or tile's decode on resource grounds as a 'cannot establish' ground, and since no other violation was established anywhere in the file, the verdict is fixed as cannot establish rather than nonconforming. Separately, §5.2/§9.7 state that where the verifier declined a layer on resource grounds and so never enumerated its claimants, the walk is incomplete and the slack total 'is reported as partial.'
B's reasoning: [R-CNF-11] makes 'cannot establish' available to a traversal that declines a tile's decode on resource grounds and establishes no other violation. [R-CNT-21] specifically distinguishes a declined tile decode (walk stays complete, claimant still enumerated from its index entry) from a declined layer decode or a scope-level rejection (which leave the walk incomplete/partial).
findings.quotation_a: cannot establish is available only to a traversal that established no violation
findings.quotation_b: a tile's or a document's decode declined leaves the walk complete, that claimant being enumerated from its index entry or extent slot

findings.title: Slate B quizb-09: the editions' takers answer differently
findings.detail:
QUESTION: A layer's tile-index entry has offset = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF (the sentinel value) and length = 100 (not the sentinel value), with crc = 0. Per the document's entry-classification table, what outcome class applies to this entry (name it exactly)? Is this classification one the document calls 'structural', or does it instead leave the entry 'well-formed'? Consequently, does this entry contribute a claimant to a verifier's coverage-walk enumeration, or do the bytes it nominally addresses fall to slack?
FROM A: Outcome class: reject-tile. This is a structural classification (not 'well-formed'). Consequently the entry contributes no claimant; the bytes it nominally addresses fall to slack. [high] cites §15.3 [R-IDX-03] entry-validity table; §5.2 [R-CNT-21]; §9.7 [R-LIF-08]
FROM B: reject-tile; structural; falls to slack. [high] cites §15.3 [R-IDX-03] (entry-validity table and preamble); §21.4 register row T7
A's reasoning: offset=sentinel, length≠sentinel matches the §15.3 table row 'offset = S ∧ length ≠ S, or offset ≠ S ∧ length = S' which is marked *structural*: reject-tile, independent of the crc field's value. [R-IDX-03] explicitly states structural-ground entries are excluded from the coverage walk and their bytes fall to slack rather than contributing a claimant.
B's reasoning: Offset=sentinel, length≠sentinel is exactly the §15.3 row 'offset = S ∧ length ≠ S, or offset ≠ S ∧ length = S' marked *structural*: reject-tile (register row T7). Structural rows contribute no claimant, so the nominally-addressed bytes fall to slack.

findings.quotation_b: Such an entry contributes no stored extent to the *verifier* rows ... and none to `[R-LIF-08]`'s coverage walk, so any bytes it nominally addressed that no other claimant claims fall to slack.

findings.title: Slate B quizb-10: the editions' takers answer differently
findings.detail:
QUESTION: A layer stored at least one tile in the generation an appender's commit supersedes. That layer is planar with channels declared in order (p, q, r). The commit's only change to this layer is to insert a new channel 's' into the channel list between 'q' and 'r' — that is, not at the end of the list. Is this change one an appender may make to this layer within a single commit, or does achieving it require treating the result as a new layer (under a different name) or performing a whole-file rewrite?
FROM A: Not permitted — requires a new layer or a whole-file rewrite. [high] cites §20.3 step 4 [R-WRT-04]
FROM B: not permitted as an appender commit — requires a new layer or a rewrite. [high] cites §20.3 step 4, fixed-declarations paragraph
A's reasoning: Because the layer stored a tile in the superseded generation, §20.3 step 4's fixed-declaration bar applies. The only permitted planar-channel-list edits are extension at the end or shortening from the end; insertion in the middle of the list (between q and r) is explicitly enumerated among the changes that require treating the result as a new layer or a rewrite.
B's reasoning: §20.3 permits only extending or shortening a planar channel list at its end (not both in one commit); every other channel-list change, inserting or removing a channel anywhere but the end included, is explicitly named as requiring a new layer or a rewrite when the layer stored a tile in the superseded generation, which this layer did.

findings.title: Slate B quizb-12: the editions' takers answer differently
findings.detail:
QUESTION: A file's directory region, taken as a byte sequence, has a final 4 bytes that correctly equal the CRC-32C of the preceding dir_length − 4 bytes. However, this same file's trailer declares version_major = 2, a major value the reader does not implement (version_major is not 0). Following the document's mandated order for validating a file's trailer and its stated open-algorithm step ordering, does a conforming reader ever reach the point of fetching and verifying this directory region's CRC for this file? Answer yes or no, and name the step or rule at which the reader's processing stops.
FROM A: No. The reader's processing stops at the version gate, during trailer validation (§6.2/§6.3, governed by [R-CNT-07]), before the directory step is ever reached. [high] cites §6.2 [R-CNT-06]; §6.3 [R-CNT-07]; §19.1 steps 2-3
FROM B: No; the reader stops at the version gate (§6.3, [R-CNT-07]), during trailer validation, before the directory step. [high] cites §6.2 [R-CNT-06] (mandated validation order); §6.3 [R-CNT-07]
A's reasoning: The open algorithm's ordered trailer validation (step 2, §19.1) places the version gate before the remaining field gates and before the directory fetch (step 3). version_major=2 is a major the reader does not implement (and is not 0), so [R-CNT-07] rejects the file at the version gate within step 2, well before step 3 would fetch and CRC-check the directory region. The directory's own CRC being correct is therefore never reached or verified.
B's reasoning: The version gate is validated before dir_offset/dir_length are acted on and long before the directory region (§7.1) is fetched at all. version_major=2 is a major the reader does not implement, so [R-CNT-07] rejects the file at the version gate; the directory CRC step is never reached regardless of the directory's own correctness.
findings.quotation_a: A reader MUST validate, in order: the trailer magic; the trailer CRC; the version gate (§6.3) ... and then, those gates passed, MUST validate all of the following
findings.quotation_b: A reader MUST validate, in order: the trailer magic; the trailer CRC; the version gate (§6.3) ... and then, those gates passed, MUST validate all of the following before acting on the fields involved

findings.title: Slate B quizb-15: the editions' takers answer differently

QUESTION: Among the eight numeric identifier spaces the document's registry section tabulates (record type, channel layout, linearization, sample type, codec, filter, index encoding, metadata encoding), exactly one is defined with no experimental range at all. groups.title: Ignore-lane 'MUST NOT clear them' clause dropped from §6.3, but §6.2's unchanged table restates it

groups.location_b: §6.3, R-CNT-08: 'An updater MUST copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits of its input file, MUST NOT set any other' (middle clause gone)
groups.byte_level_rationale: §6.2's trailer flags-field table row is byte-identical in both editions: 'bits 16–31 (ignore lane) 0 from a creator, carried forward unchanged by every updater (appender and rewriter alike)'. 'Carried forward unchanged' already forbids clearing a set bit; no implementation satisfying that unchanged obligation could clear a bit and still conform, in either edition.
groups.recommended_action: No edit needed to B; the dropped clause was a redundant restatement of an obligation §6.2's table (unchanged) already states in full.

groups.title: Appender step-2's 'save where §20.4 licenses the drop' exception dropped, creating an unqualified prohibition that conflicts with §20.4's unchanged MAY-drop licence
groups.location_a: §20.3 step 2: '...MUST NOT drop the record save where §20.4 licenses the drop.'
groups.location_b: §20.3 step 2: '...MUST NOT drop the record.' (no exception)
groups.byte_level_rationale: Confirmed in both editions: A's step 2 explicitly excepts a §20.4-licensed drop; B's step 2 states the prohibition unqualified. §20.4 itself, unchanged in both editions, explicitly states 'an appender MAY drop the record in any commit it is otherwise free to make' for a PE=0 record. Unlike a case of mere restatement, 'MUST NOT drop X' does not entail an exception for later-licensed drops — the carve-out is substantive, not redundant. An appender built strictly from B's ordered, imperative step 2 has genuine textual grounds to retain a PE=0 record that a B-built appender reading only §20.4, or any A-built appender, would drop — different directory bytes for the identical requested commit.
groups.recommended_action: Restore the exception clause to B's §20.3 step 2 (e.g. 'save where §20.4 licenses the drop') so it no longer contradicts §20.4's own MAY-drop rule.

groups.title: Worked example's index-region byte total: A correctly states 644, B states an arithmetically wrong 664, inside a non-normative Example block
groups.location_a: §20.3, worked Example: '...the layer's full new index region (32 · 20 + 4 = 644 bytes...)'
groups.byte_level_rationale: 32×20+4=644, matching A and matching [R-CNT-16]'s formula 'extent_length MUST equal entry_count × 20 + ⌈entry_count / 2¹⁶⌉ × 4', which is byte-identical, unchanged, and correct in both editions. [R-CNF-01] (byte-identical in both) makes any text 'labeled Note, Example, or Rationale' non-normative, and this figure sits inside a block headed '**Example.**' in both editions. A conforming implementation, built from either edition's actual (normative) sizing rule, computes 644 regardless of edition; only a human trusting the Example's own printed total rather than deriving it would be misled, and only in B. Several inputs (adv-02, swba-02) claim byte-level effect via a hypothetical fixture-builder who ignores the normative formula — that is a claim about a human's error, not about what two correctly-built implementations of A vs. B would emit or accept, which is the actual byte-level test.

groups.location_b: §20.4, same location: 'Its MU = 1 row reaches every type, implemented or not ... so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites'

An updater built from B's literal, changed premise has textual grounds to apply the MU=1 row's 'MUST NOT modify the scope' obligation even to an implemented type's record (refusing an edit that A's — and B's own concluding clause's — reading permits via the PE bit alone), a genuine accept/reject divergence for a record whose type is implemented but whose governing flags carry MU=1, outside the specific scenarios the walk probes tested.
