result.notes: Correctness-lens summary: of 31 groups covering all 67 findings, 2 groups carry a confirmed byte-level LOSS (appender-drop-carveout-lost; mu1-row-reach-flip-contradiction) — both are genuine, verified textual differences between the editions with real accept/reject or output-byte consequences. 2 more groups are content-level LOSSes that do not reach the byte-level bar on close reading (worked-example-644-vs-664, non-normative under R-CNF-01 with the governing formula unchanged and correct in both editions; f19-register-instances-narrowed, resolved by §21.1's own unchanged precedence rule plus the unqualified, unchanged R-CNT-08 prose). 1 group (layer-drop-mu1-blocker-sentence-deleted) is graded EQUIVALENT on close reading rather than the LOSS several inputs proposed, because the specific sentence removed from B is an explicit restatement of an unchanged table row a few sentences earlier in the same section — I flag it 'clarity' severity since B's local paragraph reads more permissively in isolation even though the governing rule survives. 1 group (ignore-lane-must-not-clear-dropped) is EQUIVALENT because the deleted clause is strictly redundant with an unchanged §6.2 table cell. 2 quiz-matrix groups (quiza-06, quizb-08) are REPORTER_ERROR: in both cases the two editions' cited text is confirmed byte-identical, and one taker demonstrably misread it (in quizb-08's case, missing an explicit tile-vs-layer distinction stated once, identically, in both editions). All remaining groups (writera-01/02, verifiera-*, verifierb-*, readera-01/readerb-01, the V1-V6 cmp-verifier confirmations, and 9 of the 11 quizb items plus 2 of 3 quiza items) are EQUIVALENT: in every one I directly re-fetched the cited passage from both edition files and found it byte-identical, so whatever ambiguity or agreement the walk/quiz reports, it is not a fidelity divergence between A and B. I downgraded several inputs' 'BYTE-LEVEL' tags specifically because their rationale relied on an incompletely-built implementation (reading one register cell in isolation, or trusting a non-normative Example's stated number) rather than the totality of each edition's own normative text, including its own internal precedence/non-normativity rules — those inputs describe a real risk to a careless implementer or vector-author, but not a divergence between two implementations each correctly and completely built from their own edition.

result.disclosure: Read only the two permitted edition files in full plus a complete `diff -u` between them (no transcript-*.md files were needed or opened). No material was pre-loaded into context before I began beyond the task's own findings text, which I treated as claims to verify, not evidence. I verified every group's textual claim directly against both edition files with grep/sed/diff, quoted below and in the transcript. The decisive step was a full-file diff of the two ~5000-line editions, which showed exactly six real textual hunks total; every one of the 67 findings either traces to one of those six or reports no textual difference at all (including all 14 quiz-matrix items, none of whose cited passages fall inside any of the six hunks) — which let me grade those 14 as REPORTER_ERROR with certainty rather than by inference from prose alone. groups.title: §20.3 step 2 loses the exception for §20.4-licensed drops, contradicting §20.4's own MAY-drop license
groups.location_a: §20.3 step 2: '...MUST NOT drop the record save where §20.4 licenses the drop.'
groups.location_b: §20.3 step 2: '...MUST NOT drop the record.' (no exception)
groups.byte_level_rationale: An appender built strictly and procedurally from B's step 2 (an unqualified prohibition in a numbered MUST-in-order list) has no in-line basis to drop a carried-forward record, including one §20.4 (unchanged in both editions: 'an appender MAY drop the record in any commit it is otherwise free to make') explicitly licenses it to drop. On a commit whose only requested edit is dropping such a record (or a droppable layer), a B-only implementation following step 2 literally retains that record's header/extent slot (and, for a layer, its sub-records and index region) where an A-only implementation drops them and reclaims the slot — different directory bytes for the identical input and requested edit.
groups.recommended_action: Restore the exception clause to B's step 2, e.g. '...and MUST NOT drop the record, save where §20.4 licenses the drop.'

groups.title: §20.4's MU=1 row reach inverted in B ('every type, implemented or not'), contradicting B's own next clause
groups.location_a: §20.4, prose before the updater-obligation table: 'Its MU = 1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement — ... — so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites:'
groups.location_b: §20.4, same location: 'Its MU = 1 row reaches every type, implemented or not — ... — so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites:'
groups.byte_level_rationale: B keeps A's conclusion ('only the PE bit bites' for an implemented type) verbatim while inverting the premise it depends on, so B is self-contradictory where A is coherent. The scenario is reachable, not academic: [R-CNT-12] (unchanged, both editions) forbids only MU=1 with PE=0, so MU=1 with PE=1 is legitimate, and an updater implementing an unregistered type it defines itself (this same paragraph's own example) can hold such a sub-record. Under A, the MU=1 row does not reach it, so the row's layer-drop block does not apply; a B-built updater that takes its own literal first clause at face value would apply that block anyway, refusing a whole-layer drop an A-built updater performs on the same input and commit.
groups.recommended_action: Revert B's clause to A's: 'Its MU = 1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement', which is what B's own retained conclusion requires.

groups.title: Worked example restates 32·20+4 as 664 instead of 644 (non-normative, formula itself unchanged and correct)
groups.location_a: §20.3 worked Example: '...the layer's full new index region (32 · 20 + 4 = 644 bytes...)'
groups.byte_level_rationale: 32×20+4=644, so B's figure is a plain arithmetic error; A's is correct. But this sits inside a block labeled 'Example.', which [R-CNF-01] (identical, unchanged) makes non-normative, and the general sizing rule [R-CNT-17] (entry_count×20+ceil(entry_count/2^16)×4) that actually governs conforming output size and the L22 cross-check is unchanged and correct in both editions. A writer or verifier built strictly from either edition's normative formula computes 644 regardless of edition; only a human hand-deriving a fixture from the illustration, rather than the formula, could be misled. No implementation's bytes or accept/reject verdict differs by edition here.
groups.recommended_action: Correct B's Example to read 644, matching the unchanged formula and edition A.

groups.title: Register row F19's Instances cell narrows to 'bits 0-7', disagreeing with its own unchanged Condition cell and [R-CNT-08]
groups.location_a: §21.2 row F19, Instances cell: 'flags bits 0-15' (matches Condition cell and [R-CNT-08])
groups.location_b: §21.2 row F19, Instances cell: 'flags bits 0-7' (Condition cell and [R-CNT-08] unchanged, still bits 0-15)
groups.byte_level_rationale: §21.1 (unchanged, both editions) states the Instances column 'enumerates what a conformance corpus builds for that row' (test-vector coverage, [R-VEC-02]/[R-VEC-03]) — it is not the row's statement of the check itself, which is the Condition cell plus the governing rule. F19's Condition cell and [R-CNT-08] are byte-identical and unqualified over bits 0-15 in both editions, as is §6.2's flags-field table. A verifier that implements the Condition text and [R-CNT-08] as written — the only normative path — rejects a file with, e.g., bit 10 set, under either edition; adv-04's constructed counter-file is caught by both. The defect is confined to the register's own internal self-consistency and its stated conformance-corpus coverage promise, not to any conforming implementation's accept/reject behavior.
groups.recommended_action: Correct B's F19 Instances cell back to 'flags bits 0-15' to match its own Condition cell and restore full test-vector coverage of the incompat lane.

groups.title: B drops the standalone 'MUST NOT clear them' clause for an updater's ignore-lane bits
groups.location_a: §6.3 [R-CNT-08]: 'An updater MUST copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits of its input file, MUST NOT clear them, and MUST NOT set any other...'
groups.location_b: §6.3 [R-CNT-08], same location: '...MUST copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits of its input file, MUST NOT set any other...'
groups.byte_level_rationale: 'Copy forward X' is itself the duty to reproduce X's values unchanged; clearing a set bit is not copying it forward, so B's remaining text already forbids clearing. This is independently confirmed by §6.2's flags-field table (line 838, byte-identical in both editions): ignore-lane bits are 'carried forward unchanged by every updater (appender and rewriter alike)' — an unqualified obligation present, unchanged, in both editions regardless of §6.3's wording. No implementation conforming to either B's remaining §6.3 clause or the unchanged §6.2 table could clear such a bit.
groups.recommended_action: No behavioral fix needed; optionally restore the clause in B purely for redundant clarity, since a reader who skips the §6.2 table could otherwise be briefly unsure.

result.reasoning:
I tried three lines of attack against the EQUIVALENT grade before accepting it.

1. Logical-entailment check (does "copy forward" alone already forbid clearing?). I considered whether "copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits" could be read narrowly — as an obligation to propagate signals it recognizes while staying silent about bits an implementation regenerates from internal state (e.g. an updater that rebuilds the flags word from its own feature model and simply never sets a bit it doesn't track, rather than "clearing" it as an act). Under that narrow reading, B's remaining text ("copy forward ... MUST NOT set any other") would NOT by itself preclude an implementer from zeroing an unrecognized bit during regeneration — this is a real, non-trivial ambiguity, and it's the correct basis for cmp-reader-01's LOSS claim if §6.3 were the only place the rule lived.

2. Whole-document check (is the ambiguity actually closed elsewhere, unchanged, in the main body — not merely in a Note/Example/Rationale, which R-CNF-01 would disqualify). I ran a full `diff` of the two complete files. The *entire* difference between edition A and edition B, everywhere in the document, is five hunks (908-909 flags clause; 3219-3220 drop-record caveat; 3400 an arithmetic figure; 3497-3514 an MU=1/PE scope wording pair; 3863 "bits 0-15" vs "bits 0-7"). Nothing else differs. In particular §6.2's trailer table row (line 838 in both) is byte-for-byte identical in A and B:
   `bits 16–31 (ignore lane) 0 from a creator, carried forward unchanged by every updater (appender and rewriter alike), a set bit ignored (§6.3)`
   This sits in the normative table of §6.2 (a `structural`-class field row, not inside a `>` Note/Rationale/Example block), so it is not disqualified by R-CNT-08's own [R-CNF-01] carve-out. "Carried forward unchanged" is unambiguous in exactly the place "copy forward" was ambiguous: "unchanged" directly forecloses the regenerate-and-incidentally-zero reading that motivated attack #1. Since every ignore-lane bit is "unknown" under this format version (§6.3 itself: "no writer under this text originates an ignore-lane bit, this text defining none for it to mean anything by"), the table's blanket "ignore lane" language covers exactly the same bit population as §6.3's "unknown ignore-lane bits" — there is no scope gap between the two passages that would let B's writer satisfy the table while still clearing a bit.

3. Appendix-restatement check (looking for a fig-leaf that shouldn't count). I also found the exact same three-part obligation ("clears none and sets no other") restated verbatim, unchanged, at Appendix H (`### Appendix H — Conformance checklists (non-normative)`), and a two-part restatement in the normative §20.3 append-procedure step 6 ("unknown ignore-lane flag bits copied forward and no other set") that mirrors B's own two-clause pattern rather than curing it.
